lessons.plain: Before a big program gets funded, someone has to check that it actually serves the organization's larger direction. Think of a company's strategic plan as its map of where it wants to go, its vision as the picture of the future it hopes to reach, and its mission as its ongoing purpose. A program is a set of related projects run together to deliver a bigger change. Assessing initial objectives, requirements and risks means asking, for each one, whether it pushes the organization toward that map and purpose, or whether it only sounds good. A tidy document can still point in the wrong direction, so the real test is the connection between the program and the strategy, not the paperwork.
lessons.guessPrompt: A program proposal lists twelve requirements, a clear budget, and a full risk register, and the sponsor says it is aligned with the company strategy. What single check would most convince you that claim is true?
lessons.teach:
Definitions first. A strategic plan is the organization's chosen set of priorities for the next few years. Its vision is the future state it wants to reach, and its mission is its ongoing purpose. A program objective is a result the program must achieve. A requirement is a condition the delivered outcome must meet. A risk is an uncertain event that could push the program away from its objectives if it happens. Alignment means that every program objective traces to a strategic priority, every requirement supports at least one objective, and every significant risk is judged by whether it threatens the strategic result, not only the schedule.

Why it works: a strategy only matters if money and effort flow toward it. Following the links in the chain shows whether spending is really moving the organization in its chosen direction. A polished document cannot show that by itself.

Worked example. A regional transport firm has a strategic priority to cut customer complaints by 20 percent. Its proposed program objective is to replace the ticketing system. Step one: does the objective trace to the priority? It does only if the team can state how the new system will reduce complaints. Step two: take a requirement, a supervisor dashboard showing ticket counts by hour. It supports the objective only indirectly, so it is a candidate to challenge. Step three: take a risk, vendor delays. It threatens the schedule, so ask whether it also threatens the complaint target, and by how much. The result is a short list of unsupported requirements and unowned risks, not a simple yes or no.

Common mistake: treating a complete business case as proof of alignment. Completeness shows the paperwork is in order. It does not show the program serves the strategy.

Consequence: a program not traced to strategy can deliver every requirement on time and still leave the complaint rate unchanged. The benefits never arrive, and the funding becomes hard to justify later.

questions.prompt: A city water utility has a strategic priority to cut unplanned pipe outages by 15 percent over three years. Its proposed program installs acoustic leak sensors on 40 water mains, with the objective of detecting leaks within 24 hours. Step 1 is done: the objective traces to the priority, because faster detection shortens repair time and so cuts outage hours. Step 2 is done: the requirement that sensors cover the mains with the most past outages supports the objective directly. Step 3 is done: the risk that the sensor supplier ships late is logged as an uncertain event that could delay the program. Step 4 has not been done. Which completion does step 4 require?
choices: Estimate how many extra outage hours a delay would add against the 15 percent target, not just whether the install date slips.
Check whether the supplier contract has a late-delivery penalty, since that settles the program's risk.
Approve the risk as acceptable because the business case already lists a mitigation section.
Remove the risk from the register, since a supplier delay only affects the schedule and not the strategy.
questions.why: Significant risks must be judged by whether they threaten the strategic result, so the delay has to be measured against the outage target, not only the schedule.

questions.prompt: A regional hospital has a strategic priority to shorten emergency department waits. Which statement best describes alignment for this program's business case?
choices: The risk register lists at least twenty risks, and each one has a named owner.
The schedule has been reviewed by the portfolio board and shows no critical delays.
Every requirement is written in measurable terms and signed off by the finance office.
Every program objective traces to a strategic priority, every requirement supports an objective, and significant risks are judged against the strategic result.
questions.why: Alignment is defined by the links from strategy to objectives, requirements, and risks, not by documentation quality or schedule status.

questions.prompt: A school district's business case is complete: the charter is signed, costs are estimated, and risks are logged. Its objective is to install new attendance software. The district's strategy is to raise reading scores by 8 points. What does the business case's completeness tell you?
choices: That the attendance software needs no further justification and can start now.
That the paperwork is in order, but the link between the attendance objective and the reading priority is still unshown.
That the program is aligned, because a complete business case is the standard proof of alignment.
That the software will raise reading scores once it is installed, since every section is filled in.
questions.why: A complete business case shows the paperwork is in order but does not show that the program serves the strategy, so the missing link to reading scores remains unproven.

questions.prompt: A university has a strategic priority to raise graduate retention by 5 points. A proposed program includes a requirement for a campus map app. No program objective mentions retention. What should the program manager do with this requirement?
choices: Challenge it as unsupported, because it does not support any objective that traces to the retention priority.
Keep it, since maps may help retention indirectly and indirect support is enough.
Keep it, since any feature that helps students is a valid part of the strategy.
Move it to the schedule risk register so the team can track its delivery.
questions.why: A requirement must support at least one objective that traces to strategy, and this one supports none, so it is a candidate to challenge.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says that because the program's business case is complete and well written, the program must be aligned with the company's strategy. Explain to them, in your own words, why that conclusion does not follow, what you would check instead, and one limit of your check.
lessons.modelAnswer: A complete business case shows the paperwork is in order, but it does not show that the program serves the strategy. I would start from the strategic priorities and check that each program objective names how it moves one of them. Then I would look at each requirement and ask which objective it supports; a requirement that supports nothing is a candidate to cut or challenge. Finally I would test each risk against the strategic result, not only the schedule or budget, because a risk can be minor for the project and still threaten the outcome the strategy cares about. One limit of this check is that it depends on the strategic plan being clear and current. If the priorities are vague, the traceability will look convincing but rest on weak ground, so I would confirm the plan with the executive owner first.
rubricPoints: Completeness of documents is not the same as alignment with strategy
Trace each program objective to a named strategic priority
Test each requirement for the objective it supports
Judge risks by their threat to the strategic result, not only the schedule
Name a limit, such as an unclear or outdated strategic plan

suggested.rationale: Judging alignment means reasoning through a realistic business case, so a scenario-based exercise adds the most beyond reading, and no listed mission covers strategy traceability directly.

lessons.plain: Before a program gets real money, its leaders need a rough picture of what it will do and what it will cost. A high-level roadmap is a simple timeline of the big phases and milestones, not a day-by-day plan. A preliminary estimate is a deliberately rough figure for cost and effort, given as a range with its assumptions stated. Executive sponsor validation means the senior leader who will own the program's funding and results reviews those two things and confirms they are believable enough to proceed. This lesson covers how those pieces are built and how the sponsor's sign-off is earned.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a sponsor asked you for the cost of a program whose scope is not yet defined, what would you give them, and why could a single exact number be a risk?
lessons.teach:
A high-level roadmap is a sequence of major phases and milestones laid out over time, showing what must happen in what order and roughly when. A preliminary estimate is an early, deliberately approximate figure for cost and effort, usually given as a range with its assumptions written down. The executive sponsor is the senior leader accountable for the program's funding and outcomes. Validation is that sponsor's confirmation that the roadmap and estimate are credible enough to fund the next step.

Why it works: a sponsor cannot judge a program from its ambition alone. A roadmap shows sequencing and dependencies, and a range shows how much uncertainty the team admits. Together they let the sponsor decide whether to commit, and they set expectations that later detail can refine rather than overturn.

Worked example: a team proposes consolidating three customer-support tools into one. Step 1: they lay out phases of assessment (three months), tool selection (two months), and migration in two waves (six months). Step 2: they estimate cost from two comparable past migrations, arriving at a range of 1.2 to 1.6 million, with stated assumptions that training is included, no new hardware is needed, and a 15 percent contingency applies. Step 3: the sponsor asks which assumption carries the most risk, and the team names data migration. Step 4: the sponsor validates the roadmap and approves funding for the assessment phase only, with the full estimate to be refined after it.

Common mistake: presenting one precise number with no range or assumptions, then treating it as a promise. When discovery later reveals a higher cost, the sponsor has been committed to a figure that was never meant to be firm, and trust in the whole program drops.

An unvalidated estimate can quietly become the budget, so validation is what records the agreed range and the conditions attached to it. Validation is a decision point, not a formality, and a program without it has no agreed basis for spending.

questions.prompt: A regional water utility wants to replace 40,000 aging residential meters with smart meters that report usage remotely. Step 1: the team lays out a pilot phase (four months, 2,000 meters in one district) followed by a full rollout in four regional waves (nine months). Step 2: the team estimates cost from two comparable utility upgrades and gives a range of 3.0 to 3.8 million, with stated assumptions that existing meter contracts can be reused, no civil works are needed, and a 10 percent contingency applies. Step 3: the executive sponsor asks which assumption carries the most risk, and the team names the age of the current meter base. Step 4 is missing. What should happen next?
choices: The sponsor approves the full 3.8 million immediately so the rollout can start on schedule.
The sponsor validates the roadmap and estimate, records the 3.0 to 3.8 million range with its conditions, and approves funding for the pilot only, with the full estimate refined after it.
The team replaces the range with a single midpoint of 3.4 million so the budget is easier to track.
The team skips validation because a preliminary estimate is not expected to be firm enough for a sponsor decision.
questions.why: Validation is the sponsor's recorded decision that the roadmap and range are credible enough to fund the next step, and here that means funding only the pilot while the estimate is refined.

questions.prompt: In this course's terms, what best describes a preliminary estimate?
choices: A final budget approved by the executive sponsor after all detailed design is complete.
A list of every task in the program with its duration, without any cost information.
An early, deliberately approximate figure for cost and effort, given as a range with its assumptions written down.
A single exact cost figure that the team commits to once the business case is signed.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a preliminary estimate as an early approximate range for cost and effort with its assumptions stated, which is exactly the second option.

questions.prompt: A program team gives its sponsor one precise cost of 2.1 million with no range and no assumptions. Six months later discovery shows the true cost is about 3 million. Which lesson from this situation is most accurate?
choices: The overrun is mainly a problem of scheduling, not of how the estimate was presented.
Presenting one precise number without a range or assumptions makes it look like a promise, so the sponsor is committed to a figure never meant to be firm.
The sponsor should have asked for a longer roadmap, because longer roadmaps always produce more accurate costs.
The team was right to give one number, because sponsors prefer single figures they can track.
questions.why: The core failure is presenting a single number without the range and assumptions that show its uncertainty, which causes the sponsor to treat it as a commitment.

questions.prompt: A sponsor says the team's estimate is only preliminary, so no formal validation is needed before the team starts spending. Why is this reasoning flawed?
choices: Because an unvalidated estimate can quietly become the budget, and without validation there is no agreed basis for spending.
Because preliminary estimates are always wrong, so validation is needed to fix their numbers before any spending starts.
Because the sponsor must approve the business case first, and validation happens only after the program closes.
Because validation is only required for programs above a certain size, and this program is small.
questions.why: The teaching text says validation records the agreed range and conditions, and that a program without it has no agreed basis for spending, even when the estimate is preliminary.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a high-level roadmap and a preliminary estimate differ from a detailed plan, and why the executive sponsor's validation matters before work continues. Name one limit or tradeoff of relying on an early estimate.
lessons.modelAnswer: A high-level roadmap shows the major phases and milestones in order and roughly when they happen, while a detailed plan schedules individual tasks and owners. A preliminary estimate gives a cost and effort range built from comparable past work, with its assumptions listed, so it is honest about uncertainty. The executive sponsor validates both before work continues because the sponsor owns the funding and must agree the direction is worth committing to. Validation records the agreed range and any conditions, such as funding only the next phase. The main tradeoff is that an early estimate is wide and built on assumptions, so it can be wrong in ways that only show up after discovery. That is why the sponsor should expect the estimate to be refined and should be told in advance that the range may move.
rubricPoints: A roadmap shows major phases and milestones over time, not detailed tasks
A preliminary estimate is a range with stated assumptions, not a single firm number
The executive sponsor validates because they own funding and outcomes
An early estimate carries uncertainty that later detail can revise

suggested.rationale: An exam-style situation where the learner must judge whether a roadmap and range are credible enough for sponsor sign-off adds the most, since no listed mission or planned engine covers program governance.

lessons.plain: A business case is the written argument for spending money and effort on a program. It says what problem the program solves, what it will cost, what good it should do, and why now. Evaluating it means asking three questions: can we actually deliver this (feasibility), are we ready to start it (readiness), and does it serve what the organization is trying to achieve (strategic alignment). A business case can be tidy and well formatted and still fail all three. The skill is reading past the formatting to the reasoning underneath.
lessons.guessPrompt: A business case for a new program is neatly written, has a budget, and promises large savings. Name two things you would check before agreeing to fund it, and say why each one matters even though the document already looks complete.
lessons.teach:
A program is a group of related projects and activities managed together to deliver a benefit the organization could not get by running the projects separately. The business case is the document that justifies it: the problem, the options considered, the expected costs, the expected benefits, and the risks. Its job is to support a funding decision, so it must be judged on whether the reasoning holds, not on how polished it looks.

Three tests do most of the work. Feasibility asks whether the program can be done with the money, time, skills and technology available, given the risks. Readiness asks whether the organization is prepared to start now: sponsors named, people available, dependent systems and suppliers able to take the change, and prerequisite projects finished. Strategic alignment asks whether the program moves a stated objective in the organization's strategic plan, which is the published set of goals and priorities that leadership has committed to. A program that is cheap, ready and clearly useful can still be out of line with where the organization is heading.

Worked example. A logistics firm proposes a program to cut delivery costs by 20 percent. Step one: check the target against the strategic plan. The plan says growth in new regions is the priority, so cost cutting is a weak fit, which is a misalignment to flag. Step two: check feasibility. The cost estimate assumes a new system that has never been tested at this scale, so the estimate is fragile. Step three: check readiness. The operations director who would own the benefit has not agreed to it. The document is well formatted, yet it fails all three tests.

Common mistake: treating a complete-looking case as a sound one, or judging alignment by reading the program's own goals instead of the strategic plan. Consequence: a program funded on a weak case often stalls midway, when its benefits cannot be claimed and its sponsor moves on, leaving budget spent with little to show for it.

questions.prompt: A regional water utility proposes a program to replace 40,000 household meters with remote-reading units to cut meter-reading costs and catch unbilled water use. Step one: the strategic plan's top priority is reducing non-revenue water, which includes leaks and unbilled use, so the program serves a stated objective and alignment holds. Step two: the vendor's estimate assumes a four-year rollout, but the approved funding covers only two years, so the schedule is not feasible as proposed. Step three, the readiness check, is missing from this trace. Which step completes it?
choices: Confirm that the billing system can take the new data feed, that crews are assigned, and that a named executive has agreed to own the benefit.
Count how many meters the utility already replaced under its previous program.
Rewrite the case with a summary page and charts so the funding committee reads it more easily.
Recalculate the savings using the vendor's figures, since the vendor knows the equipment best.
questions.why: Readiness asks whether sponsors, people, dependent systems and suppliers are prepared to start now, and only the third option tests that.

questions.prompt: A city transit agency is running three separate bus route projects and a fare-system upgrade. The fare upgrade only pays off once all four are finished and managed together. Which statement best explains why this set counts as a program rather than separate projects?
choices: Because each project has its own project manager reporting to a single sponsor.
Because the agency's finance office approves all four items in a single budget line.
Because it contains four or more workstreams, which is the minimum size for a program.
Because the items are related and managed together to deliver a benefit that running them separately would not produce.
questions.why: A program is defined by related projects managed together to deliver a benefit not obtainable by running them separately, not by size, reporting lines or budget coding.

questions.prompt: A consumer electronics retailer's business case has all required sections, complete cost tables and a benefits forecast. Its readiness section notes that two key suppliers have not confirmed they can change their delivery schedules. What is the best assessment?
choices: The case passes readiness, because the document covers every required section.
The case fails the readiness test, because the program cannot start on time without those suppliers, even though the document is complete.
The case should be judged only on strategic alignment, since readiness is an operational concern.
The case passes feasibility, which is enough to offset the supplier risk.
questions.why: Readiness asks whether dependent suppliers can take the change now, and a complete-looking document does not satisfy that test.

questions.prompt: A program was funded on a business case whose benefits depend on a prerequisite project that has not yet finished. Halfway through, the team finds the benefits cannot be claimed. What is the most likely outcome, based on the consequence described for weak cases?
choices: The program switches to a cheaper option, which fixes the alignment problem.
The program stalls, its benefits cannot be claimed, its sponsor may move on, and the spent budget yields little.
The program is rescued automatically because its funding has already been released.
The benefits are delayed by a few weeks with no effect on the program's overall value.
questions.why: A case that fails readiness and feasibility tests often stalls midway, leaving budget spent with little to show for it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would tell whether a business case is genuinely aligned with the organization's strategic plan, rather than just well documented. Name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start from the strategic plan itself, not from the program's own summary. I would list the objectives leadership has committed to and then trace each claimed benefit back to one of them. If a benefit does not connect to a stated objective, the program is not aligned, however good it reads. Next I would check feasibility and readiness separately, because a program can be aligned but impossible to deliver right now. The main limit is that the strategic plan may be vague or out of date, so the trace is only as good as the plan. When that happens I would say so and ask leadership to confirm the priority before relying on the alignment claim.
rubricPoints: Traces the program's claimed benefits back to specific objectives in the strategic plan.
Distinguishes genuine alignment from the quality of the documentation.
Assesses feasibility and readiness as separate tests.
Names a limit, such as a vague or outdated strategic plan.

suggested.rationale: Judging alignment and explaining why a polished case can still fail is the core skill, and no current mission practises it.

lessons.plain: Before a program starts, its sponsors want to know what it is worth in money and in outcomes. Quantifying expected benefits means putting numbers on what the program should deliver, such as added revenue, saved cost, or fewer customer complaints. Market analysis asks how big the opportunity really is and how customers are likely to respond, so the numbers rest on outside evidence rather than hope. A high-level cost-benefit analysis then sets those expected gains against the rough costs of delivering them. Together they show how much of the work is worth doing and which parts belong in scope.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team proposes a program to build a new customer portal and says it will save 2 million a year. What three questions would you ask before you believe that number and decide how much of the portal belongs in scope?
lessons.teach:
Quantifying expected benefits means putting a number on what a program should return, before it is approved. An expected benefit is a forecast gain, such as extra revenue, cost saved, or hours returned to staff. Market analysis is the study of outside demand: how many potential customers exist, how many would actually use the offer, and what they would pay. A high-level cost-benefit analysis is a rough comparison of the program's total cost over its life against its total benefit, using estimates rather than detailed budgets. Its job at this stage is to guide scope: the parts that return more than they cost are the ones worth including.

Why it works: a benefit is only as credible as its basis. Market analysis replaces we think customers want this with counted demand, and the cost-benefit comparison forces every part of the scope to justify its price.

Worked example. A delivery firm considers same-day delivery across a service area of 40,000 households. Step 1: a survey suggests 12 percent would subscribe, which gives 4,800 subscribers. Step 2: each subscriber orders about 2 deliveries a month at a fee of 6, so yearly revenue is 4,800 times 2 times 6 times 12, about 691,000. Step 3: the estimated build cost is 1.2 million once, plus 300,000 a year to run. Over five years, benefits total about 3.46 million against costs of 2.7 million, a net gain of about 0.76 million. Step 4: the survey shows most subscribers live in two dense postcodes, so the first scope covers only those two.

Common mistake: treating the whole market as the benefit, or counting the full yearly figure from day one when adoption takes time to grow.

Consequence: if the program is sized for all 40,000 households, running costs rise with unused capacity and the net benefit can turn negative.

Rough numbers are acceptable at this stage; the purpose is a sound scope decision, not a precise forecast.

questions.prompt: A medical equipment rental firm considers a portable scanner rental service for 15,000 clinics in one region. Step 1: a survey suggests 8 percent of clinics would rent, which gives 1,200 renting clinics. Step 2: each renting clinic pays 500 a month, so at full adoption yearly revenue is 1,200 times 500 times 12, or 7,200,000. Step 3 is missing. The build cost is 4.0 million once, with 900,000 a year to run, and the team must decide how much of the region to include in the first scope. Which step completes the analysis?
choices: Divide the yearly revenue by the number of clinics to find a price per clinic, then approve the whole program if that price is above 500.
Use all 15,000 clinics as the subscriber count so that demand is not underestimated, then size the scope for that number.
Compare total benefit and total cost over the same number of years, allowing for slow adoption, and keep only the parts of the region that return more than they cost.
Add the full 7.2 million of yearly revenue to the build cost from year one, and approve the program if the total is positive.
questions.why: A high-level cost-benefit analysis compares total benefit with total cost over the same period, accounts for adoption that grows over time, and uses that result to decide which parts of the scope to include.

questions.prompt: A regional bus operator estimates that a timetable change will return 1,500 staff hours a year. Which term names this kind of forecast gain before the program is approved?
choices: Cost-benefit ratio
Expected benefit
Market analysis
Scope exclusion
questions.why: An expected benefit is a forecast gain such as extra revenue, cost saved, or hours returned to staff, estimated before approval.

questions.prompt: A public library plans a lending app for 90,000 residents. Its business case treats every resident as a certain user and counts the full estimated yearly benefit of 3 million from the first month. What is the main flaw?
choices: It should have left out the running costs and used only the build cost.
It treats the whole market as the benefit and counts the full yearly figure from day one, when adoption takes time to grow.
It uses too few residents, so the demand estimate is too low.
It relies on a documented estimate, which is never acceptable in a business case.
questions.why: The common mistake named in the teaching text is counting the whole market as benefit and counting the full yearly figure before adoption has grown.

questions.prompt: A software team has five optional modules, each with an estimated five-year benefit and cost in thousands: A 400 and 250, B 180 and 220, C 900 and 500, D 60 and 55, E 300 and 310. Using a high-level cost-benefit comparison to guide scope, which modules should be included?
choices: A, B and C, since they share a platform.
All five, since total benefit exceeds total cost.
A, C and D, since each returns more than it costs.
C only, since it has the largest benefit.
questions.why: The analysis keeps only the parts that return more than they cost: A (400 over 250), C (900 over 500) and D (60 over 55), while B and E cost more than they return.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how market analysis and a high-level cost-benefit analysis work together to define a program's scope, and name one limit of these estimates.
lessons.modelAnswer: Market analysis tells us how many people would realistically use or pay for what the program delivers, and at what price. That gives the benefit side a basis instead of a guess. The high-level cost-benefit analysis then places rough build and running costs against that benefit over the program's life. Where a part of the scope returns more than it costs, it earns a place; where it does not, it is deferred or dropped. The two work together because the market view shows where the value is, and the cost view shows which slices of that value are worth paying for. The main limit is that both rely on estimates: survey answers can overstate willingness to pay, and cost figures at this level can be off by a wide margin. So the numbers should be treated as a basis for a decision and re-checked as the program gets more detailed.
rubricPoints: Market analysis grounds the benefit forecast in counted demand and realistic adoption
A high-level cost-benefit analysis compares lifetime costs with benefits to judge each scope element
The comparison is used to decide which parts of scope to include, defer, or drop
A limit is stated, such as survey overstatement or rough cost estimates
The numbers are treated as provisional and refined as the program matures

suggested.rationale: A planned cost model engine would let the learner build a benefit and cost comparison and see how scope changes the result.

lessons.plain: A program is a set of related projects run together to deliver a larger business result. Its objectives are set by people who want something, but the program must also operate within rules: laws, industry regulations, contracts, and ethical expectations about how people and data are treated. Weighing objectives against these constraints means checking whether each goal can be pursued legally and responsibly, and noticing where a goal would need to bend or be dropped. This matters because stakeholders such as regulators, customers, employees and the public will judge the program by these rules, and an objective that breaks them creates support problems later. Done well, it keeps everyone who cares about the program agreeing on what is in bounds.
lessons.guessPrompt: A program sponsor wants to cut customer onboarding time in half by sharing customer data across three regional business units. Before any teaching, what concerns would you raise about that objective, and who would you want to hear them?
lessons.teach:
A constraint is a fixed limit a program must work within. Regulatory constraints come from rules set by regulators or industry bodies. Legal constraints come from law and binding agreements such as contracts and privacy terms. Ethical constraints are expectations of fair and honest conduct that stakeholders hold, often beyond what the law requires. An objective is the measurable result a program aims to achieve. Weighing objectives against constraints means testing each objective against all three kinds of limit and sorting it into one of three outcomes: pursue as stated, pursue with changes, or drop.

This works because constraints are not negotiable inputs. An objective that cannot be met inside them is not a real objective; it is a wish that will be blocked later, usually at great cost.

Worked example. The objective is to reduce onboarding from ten days to two by automatically approving applicants using a score built from data gathered from social media. Step one: state the objective plainly. Step two, regulatory: consumer-protection rules may require decisions that can be explained and checked for unfair outcomes. Step three, legal: privacy law and the customer terms may not allow this data to be used for that purpose without consent. Step four, ethical: declining people on data they cannot see or challenge raises fairness concerns even where the law is silent. Step five, outcome: keep the speed goal, restrict the program to consented data, add human review for declined applicants, and restate the target as four days.

A common mistake is treating a legal sign-off as the whole check, or leaving constraint review until after the business case is approved. A program that ignores these limits can be halted by a regulator or lose stakeholder trust, which forces rework and wastes the money already spent.

Constraints belong in the objective-setting step, not in the final review.

questions.prompt: A regional bus company wants to cut driver overtime from 12 percent of paid hours to 4 percent by rebuilding rosters. Transport regulators set maximum driving hours and minimum rest periods that every roster must respect. The union agreement fixes shift lengths and requires notice before any change. Step one: state the objective plainly. Step two, regulatory: rosters must respect the regulator's driving-hour and rest-period limits. Step three, legal: the union agreement limits shift lengths and requires notice before changes. Step four, ethical: rosters that leave drivers exhausted raise safety and fairness concerns even when every rule is technically met. Step five, outcome: this step is not yet decided. Which completion correctly finishes step five?
choices: Drop the program, because any change to driver rosters breaches the union agreement.
Ask the transport regulator to relax rest-hour rules so the original target can be reached.
Keep the 4 percent target and proceed, since all three checks have now been run.
Keep the overtime goal, rebuild rosters inside the rule limits, add fatigue review, and restate the target if it cannot be met.
questions.why: Step five keeps the goal where constraints allow, changes the plan to fit the limits, adds a fairness check, and resets the target if needed, which is the pursue-with-changes outcome described in the teaching text.

questions.prompt: Which description best separates a regulatory constraint from an ethical constraint?
choices: A regulatory constraint is any cost the finance team has approved, while an ethical constraint is any risk the sponsor has accepted.
A regulatory constraint applies only to public agencies, while an ethical constraint applies only to private companies.
A regulatory constraint is written in a contract, while an ethical constraint is written in a privacy policy.
A regulatory constraint comes from rules set by regulators or industry bodies, while an ethical constraint is an expectation of fair and honest conduct that often goes beyond the law.
questions.why: The teaching text defines regulatory constraints as rules from regulators or industry bodies and ethical constraints as stakeholder expectations of fair and honest conduct, often beyond legal requirements.

questions.prompt: A school district plans to cut bus route times by sharing student home addresses with a routing vendor, without asking families. Using the three-outcome method for weighing an objective against constraints, which outcome best fits?
choices: Pursue as stated, since shorter routes are a clear public benefit.
Defer constraint review until after the vendor contract is signed.
Drop the objective, since routes cannot be shortened without sharing addresses.
Pursue with changes: keep the route goal and limit data to what families agreed to share.
questions.why: The legal and ethical limits on sharing data without consent rule out the objective as stated, but the route goal itself can still be pursued if the data use is restricted to what families have agreed to, which is the pursue-with-changes outcome.

questions.prompt: A program lead gets legal sign-off on a marketing campaign and skips ethical review, reasoning that the law is satisfied. What is the main risk of this approach?
choices: No risk, because legal sign-off is the whole check and ethics is optional.
Only a fine from the regulator, with no effect on stakeholders.
The campaign will fail its legal test, so the sign-off will be withdrawn.
Stakeholders may lose trust even where the law is met, which can force rework and waste money already spent.
questions.why: The teaching text warns that treating legal sign-off as the whole check is a common mistake, because ignoring limits can cost stakeholder trust and force costly rework.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is new to program management how you would decide whether a program objective is acceptable given regulatory, legal and ethical constraints. Name one limit or tradeoff in your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by writing each objective in plain terms, then check it against three lists: the regulations that apply to the sector, the legal obligations in contracts and privacy law, and the ethical expectations of fairness and transparency that stakeholders hold even where the law is silent. For each objective I would mark it as acceptable, acceptable with changes, or not acceptable, and record the reason. Changes usually mean narrowing the scope, adding consent steps, or adding human review, and then restating the target so the benefit forecast stays honest. The main limit is that my ethical reading is a judgement rather than a rule, so I would bring in legal counsel and affected stakeholders rather than deciding alone, and I would accept that some attractive benefits may shrink or disappear.
rubricPoints: Checks each objective against regulatory, legal and ethical constraints separately
Gives a clear outcome such as pursue, pursue with changes, or drop, with reasons
Explains that changes often narrow scope or add consent or human review, and the target is restated
Names a real limit or tradeoff, such as ethics being a judgement or benefits shrinking

suggested.rationale: Explaining the tradeoff back to a teammate is the core skill here, and none of the listed missions practise constraint-based objective review.

lessons.plain: Before a large effort made of several related projects starts, the people who control the money need to say yes to it. A program charter is a short document that explains what the program is for, roughly what it will cost, the major checkpoints it will pass through, and the benefits the organization expects to get back. Leadership reads it, asks questions, and approves or rejects it. Think of it as the permission slip and the rough budget sheet in one, written before anyone spends serious time on detailed planning.
lessons.guessPrompt: A leadership team is asked to fund a three-year program costing about 4 million to replace the company's customer system. What would you expect them to need to see before saying yes, and why would a detailed 200-page project plan not be enough on its own?
lessons.teach:
A program is a group of related projects managed together to reach one strategic goal. A sponsor is the senior executive who owns the program, holds its budget, and is accountable for its results. A program charter is the document that asks leadership for approval. It gives high-level costs, milestones, and benefits, and it names the sponsor. A milestone is a dated checkpoint that marks a significant point, such as a pilot going live. A benefit is measurable value to the organization, such as money saved, revenue gained, or risk avoided.

It works because leaders decide on a few numbers and a clear line to strategy, not on every task. The charter sets a spending ceiling and a set of promises the program can later be held to. Detailed planning comes after approval.

Worked example. A logistics company proposes replacing dispatch software across three depots. Step 1: the charter states the purpose, cutting missed deliveries, which supports the goal of better service. Step 2: the cost is shown as about 3.2 million over 18 months, with the assumptions listed. Step 3: milestones are a pilot at one depot by month 6, all depots live by month 15, and a benefits review at month 18. Step 4: the benefit is a 20 percent drop in missed deliveries, worth about 0.8 million a year, with a named owner for each measure. Step 5: leadership approves the first phase and asks for a review at the pilot milestone.

Common mistake: presenting benefits as hopes with no owner or measure, or a cost with no assumptions, so approval rests on optimism. Consequence: the program is funded, the pilot misses its target, nobody is accountable for the shortfall, and the budget overruns because the ceiling was never clear.

A charter earns approval only when each figure can be traced to an assumption and an owner.

questions.prompt: A hospital network proposes a shared patient-scheduling system for four clinics. Step 1: the charter states its purpose, fewer missed appointments, which supports the goal of shorter waiting times. Step 2: the cost is about 1.1 million over 12 months, with the assumptions listed: training hours, licence count, and data migration effort. Step 3: milestones are a go-live at the first clinic by month 4 and all four clinics live by month 10. Step 4: this step is missing. Step 5: the chief operating officer is named as sponsor and the charter goes to the executive board for approval of phase one. What belongs in Step 4?
choices: Detailed scheduling designs for each clinic are drafted once the board approves the charter.
The benefit is that patients will feel the clinics are more modern, which the board can judge at the end.
The benefit is a 12 percent drop in missed appointments, worth about 0.3 million a year, with the clinic operations manager named as owner of that measure.
The total cost is restated as 1.1 million with no fixed ceiling, so the budget can be adjusted freely later.
questions.why: Step 4 in a charter states each benefit as a measurable value with a named owner, which is the only option that does both.

questions.prompt: In a program charter, what is a benefit?
choices: Measurable value to the organization, such as money saved, revenue gained, or risk avoided.
The total money set aside for the program, shown before any assumptions are listed.
The senior executive who owns the program, holds its budget, and answers for its results.
A dated checkpoint that marks a significant point in the program, such as a system going live.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a benefit as measurable value to the organization, and the other options define a milestone, a sponsor, and a budget figure instead.

questions.prompt: A library consortium's charter asks for approval of a 0.9 million cost over two years, lists three milestones, and claims the benefit is that staff will be happier. Which part of the charter most needs fixing before leadership decides?
choices: The milestones, because a go-live date should never appear in a charter.
The sponsor line, because the sponsor should be the program's project manager instead.
The benefit, because it has no measure and no named owner, so approval would rest on optimism.
The cost figure, because a charter should show costs only after detailed planning.
questions.why: A charter earns approval only when each figure can be traced to an owner and a measure, and a vague benefit like staff happiness has neither.

questions.prompt: A regional bus operator's charter shows a 2.4 million cost but gives no assumptions behind it. Once the program is funded, what is the most likely result according to the course's account of charters?
choices: The budget overruns, because the spending ceiling was never clear enough to hold the program to.
The sponsor takes over detailed planning, so the missing assumptions are filled in automatically.
Leadership reviews the cost at the first milestone and the figure is corrected without any budget change.
The program finishes early, because a cost without assumptions tends to be padded and then not fully spent.
questions.why: The teaching text says a cost with no assumptions leaves the spending ceiling unclear, and that unclear ceiling is what allows the budget to overrun.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has never written a charter what a program charter is for, and name one limit or tradeoff of approving a program on high-level numbers.
lessons.modelAnswer: A program charter is the document that asks leadership to approve a program before detailed planning starts. It gives the purpose, a high-level cost range, the major milestones with dates, and the expected benefits, and it names the sponsor who is accountable. Leaders use it to decide whether the program fits strategy and is worth funding. The main limit is that the numbers are estimates made with incomplete information, so the cost and benefit figures can be wrong. That means approval should set a ceiling and a review point, not a blank cheque. We should state the assumptions behind each figure and plan to re-check them at the first milestone, before more money is committed.
rubricPoints: Defines the charter as the document seeking leadership approval, covering purpose, costs, milestones, and benefits
States that the charter is high-level and comes before detailed planning
Names the sponsor as the accountable owner of the program
Identifies a limit: estimates rest on assumptions and can be wrong, so reviews or funding ceilings are needed

suggested.rationale: The objective is a document and decision skill, and explaining the charter and its limits back to a teammate is the core competence, while no listed mission or planned engine covers program governance.

lessons.plain: A program is a temporary group of related projects that together aim to deliver a business result. Operations are the ongoing work an organization does every day, such as running a warehouse or a support desk. An integration opportunity is a place where a program and daily operations could share something instead of each buying or building it separately: the same people with the right skills, the same building or equipment, the same budget line, or the same computer system. Spotting these early saves money, avoids duplicate work, and stops the two sides from pulling against each other. This lesson shows how to look for them across four areas.
lessons.guessPrompt: A new program will build a customer portal, and the operations team already runs a help desk that uses a ticketing system and has spare desks on its support floor. Before reading on, name two places where the program and the help desk could share something, and say why sharing would help rather than hurt.
lessons.teach: An integration opportunity is a point where a program and the organization's ongoing operations can share a resource, a decision, or a process instead of running in parallel. The four areas named in this objective are human capital (people and their skills), facilities (buildings, space and equipment), finance (budgets, cost centers and funding), and systems (software, data and IT infrastructure). A program is a group of related projects managed together to deliver a business benefit. Operations is the repeating work that keeps the business running. Programs are temporary, so they often need people, space and tools that the permanent organization already has. Operations also faces changes the program is making, such as new software or new procedures. When the two are planned together, duplicate purchases fall, skills are reused, and handoffs at the end of the program go more smoothly. Worked example: a program will replace a fleet-tracking tool. Step one, list what the program needs: two data analysts, a server environment, a budget line and a training room. Step two, ask operations for the same items. Operations has an analyst team with spare capacity, a data platform the tool could use, and a training room booked only twice a month. Step three, record each match as a candidate opportunity with an owner and a date to confirm. The program avoids buying a second server and reuses a trained analyst. A common mistake is looking only at what the program needs and never at what operations already has, which leads to duplicate builds. Another is claiming a sharing opportunity without confirming that operations has capacity or that a budget owner agrees. If two systems hold the same customer data and nobody plans the link, operations may keep an old copy while the program reports different figures, which erodes trust in both. Sharing points must therefore be checked against real capacity before they are counted as savings.

questions.prompt: A hospital group runs a program to roll out a new patient-scheduling app across six clinics. Step one: the program lists its needs, which are two nurse educators for training, a training room for four sessions a week, a funded budget line, and a reporting database. Step two: the program asks clinical operations for matching items. Operations has a training room free on Tuesdays and Thursdays, a reporting database with spare storage, and a nurse educator team that is fully booked until next year. Step three: the program records the training room and the reporting database as candidate sharing points, each with a named owner and a date to confirm. Step four is missing from the sequence. The program has not yet checked whether the Tuesday and Thursday slots and the database storage are really available, and it has not asked the budget owner to agree. Which action completes step four before the program counts any saving?
choices: Ask the room scheduler and database administrator to confirm real free capacity and ask the budget owner to agree, and count the saving only after both confirm.
Hire a third nurse educator from the program budget so the educator team is not needed.
Buy a second reporting database so the program is not dependent on operations.
Count the full cost of the training room as saved, since the program will not have to rent a room.
questions.why: A sharing point is only a saving once operations confirms real capacity and the budget owner agrees, so step four is that check.

questions.prompt: Which description best defines an integration opportunity as the term is used in program management?
choices: A point where a program and ongoing operations share a resource, decision or process instead of running in parallel.
A budget overrun that the program absorbs into its contingency reserve.
A new project that the program starts to replace a failing operational service.
Any regular meeting at which program staff and operations staff exchange status updates.
questions.why: An integration opportunity is defined as a shared point between the program and operations, not a new project, an overrun or a routine meeting.

questions.prompt: A regional transit authority's fare-card program finds that its customer-service team already uses a call-centre software licence. The program books a 40 percent saving on new licences without asking the IT team whether the existing licence has free seats for the program's staff. What is the main risk of this approach?
choices: The fare-card system will automatically fail once the program reaches its end date.
The program will be unable to report its budget to the finance cost centre at all.
The claimed saving may not exist, because a sharing point must be checked against real capacity before it is counted.
The customer-service team will be legally required to stop using its own licence.
questions.why: Counting a sharing saving without confirming real capacity can produce a saving that is not real, which the teaching text warns against.

questions.prompt: A water utility's program needs a dedicated room to store spare sensor hardware and a trained technician to install it. Which two integration areas do these two needs fall under, respectively?
choices: Systems for the room and finance for the technician.
Human capital for the room and systems for the technician.
Finance for the room and facilities for the technician.
Facilities for the room and human capital for the technician.
questions.why: Space and equipment fall under facilities, and people with their skills fall under human capital, so the pairing is facilities and human capital.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would spot integration opportunities between a new program and day-to-day operations, and name one limit or tradeoff of sharing resources between them.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by listing what the program needs in four areas: people and skills, space and equipment, budget, and systems. Then I would ask the operations leads what they already have in those same areas and where they have spare capacity or a process that overlaps with ours. Each match becomes a candidate opportunity with a named owner, a confirmed date, and the benefit it produces. The main limit is that sharing creates dependency. If the program borrows an analyst who is also needed for the operational reporting cycle, both sides can slip when demand peaks. So before committing, I would check that the shared resource has agreed capacity, that the budget owner accepts how the cost is split, and that there is a fallback if the shared item is unavailable when the program needs it.
rubricPoints: Covers the four areas: human capital, facilities, finance and systems.
Looks at both program needs and existing operational capacity before proposing a match.
Assigns an owner and confirms each candidate opportunity rather than assuming it.
Names a real limit, such as competing demand, cost-split disputes, or dependency on a shared resource.

suggested.rationale: Choosing which sharing options to pursue when resources and budgets compete is best practised as an exam-style situation to reason through, not as a single tool task.

lessons.plain: A program charter is the short founding document that officially starts a program, which is a group of related projects managed together to deliver a business result that no single project could deliver alone. It answers the basic questions: what the program is for, what is inside and outside its scope, what assumptions the team is relying on, what limits it must work within, who cares about it, and how people and money will be provided. The charter is tied to the business case, the document that justifies spending the money in the first place, so every element of the charter should trace back to a reason the organization wants the result. Think of it as the program's birth certificate and its permission slip rolled into one.
lessons.guessPrompt: A sponsor says, "Just start the program, we will sort out the scope and the money as we go." Based on what you know about why organizations write things down before spending money, what could go wrong with that approach?
lessons.teach:
A program charter is the formal document that authorizes a program and gives the program manager the authority to use organizational resources. Its core elements are scope (what the program will and will not deliver), assumptions (conditions taken to be true without proof, such as a regulator approving a rule by a certain date), constraints (fixed limits such as budget ceilings, deadlines, or required technology), stakeholders (people and groups who are affected by or can influence the program), and resource allocation (the people, funding and facilities committed to it). The business case is the justification document that says why the benefits are worth the cost; the charter must reflect it so that each scope item points at a benefit.

Why it works: a program spans several projects, and each project can drift toward its own goals. Writing one shared statement of purpose, boundaries and limits gives every project the same reference point, and gives the sponsor a basis to approve, reject or change the program later.

Worked example: A company's business case says it will cut field service call-outs by 20 percent within two years. Step one, the charter's purpose restates that benefit. Step two, scope lists the three projects that touch dispatch software, technician training and parts stocking, and explicitly excludes billing. Step three, an assumption states that the vendor's new scheduling tool will be available by month six. Step four, a constraint sets the budget at a fixed ceiling. Step five, resource allocation names the staff seconded from each department. Each element traces back to the 20 percent benefit.

Common mistake: writing a charter that lists projects and budgets but never states the benefit, so nobody can tell whether a scope change still serves the business case.

Consequence: when a constituent project asks to add a billing module, the program manager can check the charter and business case, see the request falls outside the stated scope and does not support the benefit, and escalate it rather than silently absorbing the cost.

questions.prompt: A regional hospital network's business case promises to cut 30-day emergency readmissions by 15 percent within 18 months. A trainee drafts the program charter as follows. Step one: the purpose restates the 15 percent readmission reduction. Step two: scope covers the discharge checklist project and the community nurse follow-up call project, and explicitly excludes the outpatient pharmacy ordering system. Step three: an assumption states that the regional health authority will publish revised discharge guidance by month four. Step four: a constraint fixes the budget at 2.4 million. Step five is missing and is the element that identifies who is affected by the program and who can influence it. Which entry completes the charter?
choices: Named people and groups affected by or able to influence the program, such as ward nurse managers and the readmission review board
A forecast of each project manager's personal workload
A second budget ceiling for the excluded pharmacy system
A rewritten benefit target of 10 percent to reduce risk
questions.why: The missing fifth element is stakeholders, which the teaching text defines as the people and groups affected by or able to influence the program.

questions.prompt: A manufacturing firm's program charter lists four statements. Which one is an assumption rather than a constraint or a resource commitment?
choices: The program must run on the existing plant scheduling system
The supplier will certify the new alloy by March, taken as true without proof
Two plant managers will be seconded half-time to the program
The total spend may not exceed 900,000
questions.why: An assumption is a condition taken to be true without proof, while the other three are a fixed budget limit, a required technology limit, and committed people respectively.

questions.prompt: A logistics company's business case promises to cut delivery damage claims by 12 percent. A project inside the program asks to add a driver-app GPS feature to the program's scope. What should the program manager do first?
choices: Approve the feature because the program has some unspent budget left over
Add the feature silently and report the extra cost at the end of the program
Reject the feature without review because a charter cannot change once written
Check whether the feature traces to the damage-claim benefit, and if it does not, escalate the request to the sponsor
questions.why: The charter ties each scope item to a benefit, so the manager tests the request against the business case and escalates it when it falls outside scope rather than absorbing it.

questions.prompt: A warehouse program's charter states its purpose as improving operations, lists three projects and a budget, but never states the benefit the business case claims. What is the main risk this creates?
choices: Each project must hire its own separate program manager
Scope changes cannot be tested against a stated benefit, so the sponsor has no clear basis to approve, reject or change them
The budget figure becomes unreliable and must be recalculated every week
The business case is automatically withdrawn by the finance office
questions.why: Without a stated benefit in the charter, nobody can tell whether a proposed scope change still serves the business case, which removes the sponsor's basis for decisions.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a program charter contains and how it connects to the business case, and name one limit or tradeoff of the charter that a new program manager should watch for.
lessons.modelAnswer: A program charter is the authorizing document for a program, which is a set of related projects run together to deliver a business benefit. It sets out the purpose, the scope boundaries, the key assumptions, the constraints such as budget and deadline, the stakeholders, and the resources committed. Every element should trace back to the business case, so that when someone proposes a change we can ask whether it still serves the promised benefit. The main limit is that the charter is only as good as the assumptions in it. If an assumption, such as a vendor delivering on time, turns out to be false, the charter can look sound while the program is already off track. So a new program manager should record assumptions explicitly, and review them at each stage gate rather than treating the charter as fixed once signed.
rubricPoints: Names the core charter elements: scope, assumptions, constraints, stakeholders, resource allocation
Explains that the charter is tied to and justified by the business case and its benefits
Gives a concrete example of how a scope or change decision is tested against the charter
Identifies a limit, such as assumptions going stale or scope being left vague

suggested.rationale: Charter elements and their link to the business case are reference facts best learned by reading, with the explanation exercise checking understanding.

lessons.plain: A program is a group of related projects managed together to deliver a larger business goal. Before anyone can plan that work, the goal has to be turned into two things: a scope statement, which says what the program will and will not deliver, and a roadmap, which shows in what order the pieces arrive over time. This objective is about making that translation honest by checking past experience and by tying every piece back to the benefits the organization wants to see. Think of it as moving from 'we want to be faster at getting goods to customers' to a concrete plan with boundaries and a timeline that someone could check later.
lessons.guessPrompt: A sponsor says the program should 'modernize our customer service.' Before any planning, what two things would you need to pin down to make that goal buildable, and why would you ask for them?
lessons.teach:
A program scope statement is a written description of the outcomes a program will deliver, the boundaries that limit it, and the exclusions that are named on purpose. A roadmap is a time-ordered view of when major components, projects, or benefit milestones are expected to land. A benefits realization plan describes how the business outcomes the program is meant to create will be measured, owned, and tracked after delivery. That last point matters: finishing outputs is not the same as producing the benefit.

Why it works: a strategic objective such as 'reduce customer order cycle time by 20 percent' is too vague to build against. Translating it means stating a measurable outcome with a baseline and a target, deciding which projects contribute to it, and writing down what is out of scope. Historical data, meaning records from earlier programs or projects such as actual durations, cost overruns, and adoption rates, tests whether the plan is realistic. If past similar efforts took nine months when the sponsor wants three, the gap is visible before commitments are made.

Worked example: a retailer's objective is to cut average warehouse dispatch time from 48 hours to 24 hours. Step one: state the outcome, the baseline, and the target. Step two: list the contributing projects, such as a new scanning system and a staff scheduling change. Step three: check history; the last scanner rollout took fourteen months across three sites, so the roadmap places the scanner milestone accordingly. Step four: record the benefit owner and the dispatch-time measure in the benefits realization plan, so the target is tracked after go-live. Step five: write exclusions, for example returns processing is out of scope.

Common mistake: writing the scope as a list of deliverables with no link to the outcome. The program then finishes everything on the list and the dispatch time does not move.

Consequence: in a running program, a roadmap that ignores historical durations gets re-baselined again and again, and benefits get declared delivered when only the outputs shipped. A scope tied to a measured outcome is what lets the program show whether it worked.

questions.prompt: A regional library network wants to cut average hold-pickup wait from 7 days to 3 days. Its team has already written the outcome with its baseline and target, and listed two contributing projects: self-service pickup lockers and text-message reservation alerts. Their records show that a previous locker installation took five months per branch across four branches. They have not yet placed anything on the timeline or written the benefits plan. Which action comes next to turn this into a usable roadmap?
choices: Remove the pickup-wait measure from the plan, because the library cannot control how patrons collect holds
Declare the program finished once the lockers are installed, since outputs show the work is done
Start all four branch installations in week one, because the timeline does not need to reflect history
Place the locker milestones on the roadmap using the historical five-month duration per branch, staggered across the branches
questions.why: The roadmap must reflect historical durations to be realistic, so using the five-month-per-branch record to place the locker milestones is the step that connects the plan to evidence.

questions.prompt: Which document describes how the business outcomes a program is meant to create will be measured, owned, and tracked after its outputs are delivered?
choices: A benefits realization plan
A variance log
A roadmap
A program scope statement
questions.why: A benefits realization plan covers measurement, ownership, and post-delivery tracking of outcomes, while the scope statement covers outcomes, boundaries, and exclusions, and the roadmap covers timing.

questions.prompt: A city water utility's program has a scope document listing ten deliverables, including new meters, a billing module, and a training schedule, but no baseline or target for leak-related water loss. What is the most likely consequence as the program runs?
choices: Stakeholders will automatically reduce the number of deliverables
The utility will have a stronger case for the program's success
The program can finish every listed deliverable while water loss stays unchanged, and success cannot be shown
The program will be re-baselined only once, at the final review
questions.why: A scope written as a deliverable list without a link to a measured outcome lets the program finish everything on the list without showing whether the intended benefit occurred.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm's earlier program took nine months to roll out a route-planning tool, but its sponsor now wants the same kind of tool in three months. What does the historical record most directly show?
choices: That the sponsor's three-month target is a stakeholder issue to be resolved after the roadmap is approved
That the gap between nine months and three months is visible before commitments are made, so the plan can be tested for realism
That the three-month target can be met simply by assigning more staff to the rollout
That the earlier program was a failure and its data should be excluded from the new plan
questions.why: Historical durations make the gap between past performance and the sponsor's target visible early, which lets the team test and adjust the plan before committing to it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has just joined the program how you would turn a vague strategic objective into a scope statement and roadmap using historical data and a benefits realization plan. Name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by restating the sponsor's objective as a measurable outcome, with a baseline and a target, so we know what success looks like. Then I would list the projects and deliverables that contribute to it and write explicit exclusions, so the scope has clear edges. For the roadmap, I would check comparable past projects in our records for actual durations and costs, and place milestones using those figures rather than the optimistic estimate. Each benefit gets an owner and a measure in the benefits realization plan, tracked after delivery and not just at go-live. The main tradeoff is that historical data may not match this program: if the technology or team is new, the history understates risk. So I would mark the roadmap as provisional and build in review points. That means the roadmap is a planning baseline to be revisited, not a promise.
rubricPoints: Turns the strategic objective into a measurable outcome with a baseline and a target.
Defines scope with contributing deliverables and explicit exclusions.
Uses historical data from comparable efforts to test roadmap durations and costs.
Assigns benefit owners and measures in a benefits realization plan that continues after delivery.
Names a limit, such as history not matching new conditions, and how the plan handles it.

suggested.rationale: Explaining the translation from objective to scope and roadmap in your own words to a teammate is the core skill here, and no listed mission or planned engine practises it directly.

lessons.plain: A program is a set of related projects run together to deliver a bigger business result. Two tools keep that work from getting lost. A work breakdown structure (WBS) is a tree that splits the whole program into smaller pieces, from the big outcome down to deliverables you can hand over and check. A responsibility assignment matrix is a grid that lists those pieces down one side and people or teams across the top, marking who does the work, who must approve it, who gives input, and who is kept informed. Together they answer the question everyone asks in a crisis: whose job is this, and what exactly is it?
lessons.guessPrompt: A program has three projects running in parallel, and two of them both believe they own the same integration deliverable. Before any teaching, what single planning tool would most likely have prevented that confusion, and what would it need to show?
lessons.teach:
A work breakdown structure (WBS) is a tree that splits the whole program into smaller pieces, from the outcome at the top down to deliverables, which are tangible results someone can inspect and accept. The bottom level of a branch is a work package, the unit you can estimate, assign and track. Decomposition means splitting a parent into children; the children together should cover the whole parent and nothing outside it. A responsibility assignment matrix (RAM) is a grid with work items down the side and people or groups across the top. A common form is RACI: Responsible (does the work), Accountable (owns the result and the sign-off, exactly one per row), Consulted (gives input before the work is done) and Informed (told after the fact).

Why it works: the WBS makes scope visible, so gaps show up on paper rather than during a cutover weekend, and a single accountable name stops decisions from drifting between people.

Worked example. Program outcome: live vehicle tracking across three depots. One level-2 branch is Data platform. Under it sits the deliverable Ingest service, with work packages for building the feed adapter, load testing and writing the runbook. Now build the RACI row for Ingest service. Step 1: name the one accountable owner, the platform lead. Step 2: assign Responsible to the build team. Step 3: mark security as Consulted on the feed credentials. Step 4: mark depot operations as Informed of the cutover date. Step 5: check that no row has two Accountable names and that every work package has an owner.

Common mistake: writing the WBS as a list of verbs such as 'test' or 'email vendor' instead of deliverables, or giving two people the A. Consequence: when the feed slips, nobody has the authority to decide, and the load test nobody owned gets skipped before cutover.

The WBS and RAM together are the program's answer to who does what, and a work package without a single accountable owner is a risk you have already accepted.

questions.prompt: A regional hospital network is adding electric ambulance charging. The program outcome is ambulance charging live at four sites. One level-2 branch is Charging bays. Under it sits the deliverable Charging bay ready for service, with three work packages: supply cable installation, charger mounting and wiring, and commissioning test. Trace the RACI row for that deliverable. Step 1: name one accountable owner, the facilities engineering manager. Step 2: assign Responsible to the electrical contractor crew for the first two packages, and mark the clinical transport lead as Consulted on bay location. Step 3 is missing from this trace and you must supply it: it is the check that the children of the parent together cover everything a ready bay needs, with nothing outside the parent. Step 4: mark ambulance dispatch as Informed of the outage window. Which completion of the missing Step 3 is correct?
choices: Replace the commissioning test with a deliverable named Test charger so that the tree uses outcomes rather than verbs.
Make the dispatch centre Responsible for the cutover because it owns the schedule.
Confirm the three packages together cover a usable bay. Crew training on the charge-and-handover procedure is needed but sits in no package, so add it as a fourth work package under the parent.
Give the charger vendor the Accountable role so that warranty claims are handled by one party.
questions.why: The decomposition check asks whether the children together cover the parent with nothing missing, and the crew training gap is the kind of omission this check exists to catch.

questions.prompt: A city transit program splits its WBS into branches. Which bottom-level entry is written as a deliverable rather than as an action to perform?
choices: Test readers
Negotiate fare-card contract
Send bus driver notices
Fare-card reader installed on all 40 buses
questions.why: A deliverable is a tangible result someone can inspect and accept, and only the installed-readers entry describes an inspectable result rather than a verb.

questions.prompt: A retail chain is rolling out new point-of-sale tills. For the row Till firmware package, the store systems manager and the regional IT lead are both marked Accountable. What is the correct fix?
choices: Mark both as Consulted so that neither carries the sign-off alone.
Remove the row and let the store managers decide firmware timing locally.
Keep both as Accountable but assign the Responsible role to a third person to split the load.
Keep the regional IT lead as the single Accountable owner and move the store systems manager to Responsible or Consulted.
questions.why: Each RACI row must have exactly one Accountable name so that authority to sign off is never unclear, and the regional IT lead should own the result.

questions.prompt: At a research institute, the data migration package has a named Responsible team but no Accountable name in its RACI row. The migration later fails halfway through. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: The institute's governance board adds the missing owner within the same day without any further delay.
The failure is recorded as Informed status and no action is required until the next review.
Nobody has the authority to decide whether to roll back or continue, so the failure is handled slowly and the risk was effectively accepted without an owner.
The migration proceeds automatically because the Responsible team has the authority to finish.
questions.why: A work package without a single accountable owner has no one authorised to make the decision under pressure, which is the failure mode the teaching text describes.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a program WBS and a responsibility assignment matrix work together, and name one limit or tradeoff of building them early in the program.
lessons.modelAnswer: The WBS breaks the program down from outcome to deliverables to work packages, and each level should fully cover its parent so nothing is missing. The responsibility matrix then sits alongside it: each work item gets one Accountable owner, one or more Responsible doers, and Consulted and Informed parties. I would walk through one deliverable with them so they see that the matrix is only as good as the tree beneath it. The main limit is that a WBS drawn before the design is settled tends to encode guesses, so it has to be revisited as the roadmap firms up. Ownership across constituent projects also goes stale quickly when people move, so I would review the matrix at each stage gate rather than treat it as finished.
rubricPoints: A WBS decomposes the program into deliverables and work packages, with each level covering its parent fully.
A RACI or similar matrix assigns exactly one Accountable owner per work item.
Responsible, Consulted and Informed roles are distinguished and mapped to the work.
An early WBS or RAM can encode untested assumptions and must be revisited as scope and design change.
Ownership across constituent projects needs regular review because roles and people change.
