suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine builds a program WBS or responsibility matrix, and the core skill here is explaining how the two artifacts fit together.

lessons.plain: A program is a group of related projects run together to deliver a bigger change than any one project could. An integrated program management plan is the single master document that says how those projects will be scheduled, checked for quality, watched for risk, communicated about, and staffed, and how those five areas fit together. It is not five separate plans stapled into one folder. It sets shared rules, such as one way of reporting progress and one list of dependencies, so that a delay in one project is visible to everyone who relies on it. Think of a home renovation: the kitchen, bathroom and wiring jobs each have their own checklist, but the master plan says which job must finish before the next can start.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company runs three projects that all need the same two engineers and must all finish before one customer launch. If one project slips by a month, what should the program manager check first, and why is checking only that project's own schedule not enough?
lessons.teach:
Key terms. A program is a set of related projects managed together to reach a shared business goal. Each project inside it is a constituent project. A baseline is the approved version of a plan that later performance is measured against. A dependency is a link where one piece of work cannot start or finish until another does. The integrated program management plan is the master plan that ties together five subsidiary plans: schedule (program milestones and their sequence), quality (the standard every project's output must meet), risk (how program-level threats are logged and escalated), communication (who hears what, how often, and in what format), and resources (people, budget and vendors shared across projects).

Why it works. Each project tends to optimise for its own goals. Without a common plan, every project sets its own dates, risk ratings and reporting, and the collisions stay hidden until late. The integrated plan sets common rules and a shared dependency map, so the program can see how a change in one project affects the others and the benefit the program exists to deliver.

Worked example. A transit agency runs three projects: a new fare payment system (A), a bus depot network upgrade (B), and a driver scheduling tool (C). Step 1: the schedule section records that A's cutover needs B's depot network live, so B's milestone is a gate for A. Step 2: the resources section shows one integration engineer shared by A and C. Step 3: the risk section escalates any delay to B's network work to program level, because it threatens A's cutover date. Step 4: the communication section sets one monthly status format for all three. When B slips two weeks, the program sees at once that A's cutover slips, that C loses engineer time, and that the cash-handling savings start later.

Common mistake. Writing three good project plans and placing them in one folder. The result is a bundle, not a program plan, because it has no shared dependencies and no shared resource rules.

Consequence. In a running program, the costliest failure is a hidden dependency. The fare system can be built on time and still be unusable because the depot network is late, so the benefit is delayed even though every individual project reports green.

questions.prompt: A regional retail chain runs three constituent projects: a loyalty app launch (P), a store barcode scanner rollout (Q), and a supplier invoice portal (R). The integrated program management plan is being drafted, and the team has written four steps. Step 1, schedule: P's points launch cannot go live until all 40 stores have Q's scanners running, so Q's final store milestone gates P. Step 2, resources: the same two field technicians are booked on both Q and R during March. Step 3, risk: any slip to Q's store milestone is logged at program level because it threatens P's launch date. Step 4 is missing. It should record the approved baseline date for Q's final store milestone, so that every later slip is measured against one agreed date rather than against whatever date each project chooses to report. Which option correctly completes the plan?
choices: P's launch date is moved earlier so the loyalty app is not blocked by the scanner work.
R's invoice portal is removed from the program because it shares technicians with Q.
The approved baseline date for Q's final store milestone is recorded in the schedule section as the shared reference for variance.
Each project keeps its own status date and reports it separately to the sponsor each month.
questions.why: A baseline is the approved version of a plan that later performance is measured against, so recording the approved milestone date gives the program one common reference for variance, which is the missing step.

questions.prompt: A museum runs three exhibit-building projects under one program. Which subsidiary plan within the integrated program management plan defines the standard that every project's output must meet?
choices: Resources
Risk
Schedule
Quality
questions.why: The quality subsidiary plan sets the standard every project's output must meet, while schedule covers milestones and sequence, risk covers threat logging, and resources covers shared people, budget and vendors.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm runs a fleet tracking project and a depot expansion project under one program. Each project reports green in its own status pack, yet the fleet tracking go-live is blocked by depot work that is two months late. What is the most likely gap in the program plan?
choices: There is no shared dependency map linking the two projects.
The quality standard is set too high for the depot expansion.
Each project's risk ratings were written by a different manager.
The communication plan uses a different font for each project's report.
questions.why: Without a shared dependency map, a project can look healthy while another project it depends on is late, so the hidden dependency only surfaces when it blocks delivery.

questions.prompt: A city council runs two projects under one program: a permit online portal and a records digitisation effort. Both need the same database administrator for six weeks. Which subsidiary plan in the integrated program management plan should record how this shared person is allocated across the two projects?
choices: Quality, because it sets the standard for the administrator's output.
Communication, because it decides who hears about the administrator's availability.
Resources, because it covers people, budget and vendors shared across projects.
Schedule, because it lists the program milestones and their sequence.
questions.why: A shared person is a shared resource, and the resources subsidiary plan is where the program sets the rules for people, budget and vendors used by more than one project.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says our three projects each have a solid plan, so we do not need an integrated program management plan. Explain to them what the integrated plan adds, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on a single master plan.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would say the individual project plans show how each project will deliver its own scope, but they do not show how the projects affect each other. The integrated program plan is the master document covering schedule, quality, risk, communication and resources across all three projects. Its main value is shared dependencies: if the depot network slips, we can see that the fare cutover moves and that the scheduling tool loses engineer time, and we can estimate how the benefit timing shifts. It also sets one resource rule for engineers shared between projects and one reporting format, so a status report means the same thing everywhere. The tradeoff is overhead and false confidence. A master plan takes effort to build and keep current, and if it is updated slowly it can look reliable when it is not. Each project still needs its own detail, and the master plan should be refreshed at agreed review points rather than treated as fixed.
rubricPoints: Explains that the integrated plan covers schedule, quality, risk, communication and resources together across the constituent projects
Gives the purpose of surfacing cross-project dependencies and shared resource conflicts before they hit
States that individual project plans alone do not show program-level effects on benefits
Names a real limit, such as the effort to maintain it or the risk of a stale master plan giving false confidence

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine practises building a cross-project master plan, so explaining the integration and its tradeoffs back is the core skill here.

lessons.plain: A program is a group of related projects run together to deliver a larger business result. Before the work gets going, the team agrees on a short list of numbers that show whether that result is on track, and on the dates when people will stop and look at those numbers. Those agreed numbers are the standard measurement criteria. They let a board decide to keep going, change course, or stop based on evidence rather than on how busy everyone feels.
lessons.guessPrompt: A program aims to make customers happier with support, and every one of its projects finished on time and within budget. Why might the board still be unable to tell whether the program is succeeding, and what would you ask for before the next meeting?
lessons.teach:
Standard measurement criteria are the agreed yardsticks a program uses to judge its progress. The main ones are key performance indicators, usually shortened to KPIs. A KPI is a measurable value that reflects how well an intended outcome is being achieved, such as the median number of days taken to resolve a support ticket. Each KPI needs a baseline, meaning its value before the program started, taken from historical data. It also needs a target, the value the program commits to reach by a stated date. A tolerance, sometimes called a threshold, is how far the measure may drift from target before someone must act. Success review points are scheduled decision moments, often at stage gates or after each benefit is delivered, when the board compares actual KPI values with targets and tolerances and chooses to continue, adjust, or stop.

Why it works: a number with no baseline cannot show improvement, and a target with no review date never triggers a decision. Agreeing the criteria before work starts stops the team from choosing flattering measures later.

Worked example: a program aims to shorten the time between a signed contract and the first invoice. The baseline from last year's data is a median of 42 days. The target is 25 days by month 18. The tolerance is 30 days at review point two, month 9. Step one: the data source is the billing system, extracted monthly. Step two: the owner is the finance lead. Step three: at month 9 the actual median is 38 days, which breaches the tolerance. Step four: the board does not simply note it. It requires a corrective action plan and a revised forecast.

Common mistake: choosing activity measures, such as the number of projects delivered, which can rise while the business outcome does not move.

In a running program, criteria without agreed thresholds leave variance analysis with nothing to compare against, so problems surface only at closure.

questions.prompt: A regional parcel firm starts a program to raise the share of warehouse orders dispatched on the same day they are placed. Its key performance indicator (KPI, a measurable value showing how well an outcome is being achieved) is that same-day share. The baseline (the value before the program began, from historical data) is 71 percent from last year's dispatch log. The target (the value committed to by a stated date) is 90 percent by month 12. The tolerance (how far the measure may drift from target before action is required) is 84 percent at review point two, month 6. Step one: the data comes from the warehouse management system, extracted weekly. Step two: the owner is the operations director. Step three: at month 6 the actual same-day share is 79 percent, which breaches the tolerance. What must the board do next?
choices: Lower the 90 percent target to 79 percent so the measure shows as on track
Wait until month 12 to see whether the figure recovers on its own
Require a corrective action plan and a revised forecast before the program continues
Replace the same-day share with a count of orders dispatched in total
questions.why: A breached tolerance at a success review point requires the board to act, so it must demand a corrective action plan and revised forecast rather than ignore, move the target, or swap the measure.

questions.prompt: A clinic program records that the share of appointments missed without notice averaged 18 percent in the twelve months before the program began. What term describes that 18 percent figure?
choices: A success review point
A baseline
A tolerance
A target
questions.why: A baseline is the value of a measure before the program started, taken from historical data, which is what the 18 percent represents.

questions.prompt: A library program reports that the number of community workshops it ran rose from 40 to 65 this year, and the sponsor calls this proof of success. What is the main weakness of this measure?
choices: It was never given a success review point, which makes the number meaningless
It is a valid KPI because it is a countable number
It has no tolerance, so it cannot be measured at all
It is an activity measure that can rise while the business outcome does not move
questions.why: Counting activities like workshops can increase while the intended outcome stays flat, which is the common mistake of choosing activity measures.

questions.prompt: A school district program sets a KPI of the average days between a student's absence flag and parent contact, with a baseline of 9 days, a target of 3 days by month 12, and a tolerance of 5 days at review point two, month 6. At month 6 the actual average is 6 days. What should the board do?
choices: Take no action, since 6 days is closer to the target than the 9-day baseline
Require a corrective action plan and a revised forecast, because 6 days breaches the 5-day tolerance
Stop the program immediately because the target was not reached by month 6
Raise the tolerance to 6 days so the measure shows as acceptable
questions.why: The actual value exceeds the tolerance at a review point, so the board must require a corrective plan and revised forecast rather than ignore it, move the tolerance, or stop the program at this point.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who will run the next program review how standard measurement criteria differ from project status reports, and name one limit or tradeoff of the KPIs you would agree at the start.
lessons.modelAnswer: Status reports say what the team did: tasks completed, milestones hit, risks logged. Standard measurement criteria say whether the program is delivering the outcome it was funded for. Each KPI should have a baseline from historical data, a target with a date, and a tolerance. Success review points are dated moments when the board compares actual values with those figures and decides to continue, adjust, or stop. The main tradeoff is that a KPI is only a proxy. A measure that is easy to collect, such as average response time, may improve while the customer experience does not, so I would pair it with a lagging benefit measure and agree the data source and owner up front. A few well-defined measures reviewed on schedule are worth more than a long dashboard nobody acts on.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes outcome measures (KPIs) from activity or status reporting.
Requires a baseline, a target, and a tolerance for each measure.
Ties success review points to dated decisions: continue, adjust, or stop.
Names a limit such as proxy measures or data availability.

suggested.rationale: Explaining the criteria and their tradeoffs back to a teammate is the core skill, and no listed mission or planned engine covers this objective.

lessons.plain: A program is a group of related projects managed together to reach a benefit that none of those projects could deliver alone. A kickoff is the first formal meeting, where the people who will run and support the program agree on its purpose, who makes which decisions, who does what, and how they will talk to each other. After that, the program runs feedback loops: regular updates, reviews, and requests for input that carry information back to the people who can act on it. Lessons learned are the things the team notices along the way, both what worked and what did not, written down while they are still fresh so the next project does not repeat the same mistakes. This objective is about setting up those routines and making sure the knowledge they produce is actually captured and used.
lessons.guessPrompt: A program has six projects, and the first two have already finished with some painful surprises. Before any training, what would you put in place early on so that the lessons from those surprises reach the people starting the later projects, instead of staying in one person's head?
lessons.teach:
A program is a set of related projects managed together so that a business benefit is delivered that the projects could not deliver separately. A kickoff is the formal start, where the sponsor (the executive who owns the benefit), the program manager, and the leads of each project agree on the purpose, the decision rights, the roles, and the communication plan. A communication plan lists who needs which information, how often, in what format, and who is responsible for sending it. A feedback loop is a repeating cycle in which information flows back from the work to the people who can change it, so problems are corrected early. A lessons learned log is a shared record where each entry names what happened, the cause, the effect, the action taken, and an owner for that action.

Why this works: projects inside a program learn at different speeds. Without a set routine, one project can find a fix that the others never hear about. The kickoff sets up the channels before anyone needs them, and the feedback loop keeps the log alive during the work rather than only at the end.

Worked example. A program merges three regional customer-support tools into one. At kickoff the sponsor states the goal, the program manager names the three project leads, and the group agrees on a weekly status note to the steering committee and a cross-project review every two weeks. Each project lead must add any notable event to the shared log within two working days. In month two, the first region's data migration silently drops records containing accented characters. The lead logs the cause and the fix, and assigns the data-quality owner to add a character check. At the next review, the second region's lead hears about the check before starting their own migration, so their load succeeds.

Common mistake: holding lessons learned until a closing meeting. By then the people who saw the problem have moved on, and the cause is forgotten. A second mistake is logging entries without assigning an owner who must act on them.

Consequence in a running system: if the accented-character problem were not logged and shared, the second migration would drop customer records during business hours and force a rollback. The routine is what stops that repetition.

The routine exists so that lessons reach the next project while they can still change its plan.

questions.prompt: A program joins two warehouse-automation projects, one for conveyors and one for pallet scanners. In week three the scanner project's lead finds that a firmware update makes scanners misread pallets heavier than 800 kg. The lead records the event in the shared lessons learned log within two working days, stating the cause (the new weight threshold in firmware 3.2), the effect (about 4 percent of pallets routed to the wrong bay), and the action taken (the threshold was reset to the old value). The entry is then shared at the next cross-project review. The one step not yet taken is this: the entry is assigned to ____, who must act on it. Which completion fills the blank correctly?
choices: the sponsor's signature on the program charter amendment
the program's closing report, which is written after all projects finish
the finance team, which recalculates the budget variance for the month
a named owner who will verify the threshold is correct and follow up on the action
questions.why: A lessons learned entry needs an owner for its action, and the owner is the person responsible for making sure the fix is verified and followed up, which is the step the scenario leaves out.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is a feedback loop in a program?
choices: A complete list of stakeholders with their contact details and preferred meeting times.
A monthly budget report that finance produces to show spending against plan.
A one-time sign-off form that the sponsor signs when the program closes.
A repeating cycle in which information from the work flows back to the people who can change it, so problems are corrected early.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a feedback loop as a repeating cycle that carries information from the work back to those who can change it, so problems are corrected early.

questions.prompt: A program has four projects. In month one, one project lead finds a vendor licence limit that will block a step all four projects share. The team decides to record the event only at the closing review. What is the main problem with this decision?
choices: The sponsor will need to re-sign the program charter before the closing review can record any new entries at all.
Closing reviews are not allowed to record technical causes, so the licence limit could only be handled by the vendor directly.
By closing, the other projects have already set their plans, so the lesson can no longer change them.
The entry will be too long to read at the closing review, since it would need a full page of technical detail to explain the licence terms and every affected step.
questions.why: Lessons must reach other projects while they can still change their plans, and holding them until closing removes that chance, which is the main risk the teaching text describes.

questions.prompt: A program lessons learned log has 30 entries. Each entry names what happened, the cause, the effect, and the action taken, but no entry has an owner. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: Nothing changes, because no one is accountable for acting on the logged causes.
Each project lead fixes the cause automatically in their own plan without being asked.
The log becomes a legal record that the sponsor must sign before any project can continue.
The steering committee cancels the cross-project review because the log is complete.
questions.why: The teaching text warns that logging entries without an owner who must act on them stops the log from producing change, so the causes stay unaddressed.

lessons.explainPrompt: A colleague says that once the kickoff is done, the program can run on email, and lessons learned can be collected at closure. Explain to a teammate what the kickoff must set up for ongoing communication and feedback, and name one limit or tradeoff of the routine you would recommend.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would tell them the kickoff is where the channels get agreed, not just a welcome meeting. It should fix who receives which status information, how often, and who owns sending it, and it should set up a shared lessons log with a clear entry format and an owner for each action. Feedback then runs on a fixed rhythm, such as a weekly status note and a cross-project review every two weeks, so problems surface while they can still be corrected. The tradeoff is overhead: a heavy routine takes time from people who are already busy, so I would keep meetings few and log entries short, accepting that some detail is lost in exchange for consistent capture. Waiting until closure is the bigger risk, because by then the people who saw the problems have moved on.
rubricPoints: The kickoff agrees the communication plan: recipients, frequency, format, and owner of each update.
A shared lessons log is set up early, with an entry format that names cause, effect, action, and owner.
Feedback runs on a fixed rhythm during the work, not only at closure.
A real limit or tradeoff is named, such as overhead on busy staff versus completeness of capture.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers program governance, so an exam-style scenario to reason through about kickoff and feedback routines adds the most value here.

lessons.plain: Running a program means carrying out the plan that was agreed and keeping a clear, current picture of how it is really going. A program is a set of related projects managed together to deliver benefits that no single project could deliver alone. Each project reports its own numbers: work finished, money spent, dates hit, and problems still open. Consolidating means gathering those separate reports into one program view, comparing that view with the plan, and turning the result into a short status message that leaders can act on. The real skill is noticing what the numbers mean and telling the right people early enough to change course.
lessons.guessPrompt: Three projects inside one program each report green on their own status sheet, yet the program is falling behind on the benefit it was meant to deliver. Name one reason this could happen and the first thing you would check.
lessons.teach:
A program baseline is the agreed reference plan for scope, schedule, cost and expected benefits, approved at a set point in time. A constituent project is one of the projects inside the program. A variance is the gap between what the plan said should be true at a date and what is actually true. Consolidation is the step of combining every constituent project's data into one program view, using the same definitions, dates and units for every project, so the numbers can be compared fairly.

It works because a program's leaders decide from the combined view, not from twelve separate reports. A rolled-up average can hide a single project that is failing, so the consolidated view must keep each project's variance visible while also showing the program total.

Worked example. At week 10 the baseline says project A should be 90 percent complete and have spent 90k. Step 1: collect actuals from project A: 80 percent complete and 95k spent. Step 2: compare progress, which is 10 points behind plan. Step 3: compare spend, which is 5k above plan. Step 4: check dependencies, because project B's benefit needs A's output. Step 5: report the variance and its effect on B, not just a colour.

Common mistake: reporting the program as green because the average of the project colours is acceptable. The consequence is that leaders fund project B on the strength of a summary that hides a cost and schedule overrun in A that will delay the benefit.

questions.prompt: A city water-metering program has two constituent projects and reports on a 30 June baseline date. Project Pipe's figures are as of 30 June: the baseline says 40 percent complete and 2.0 million spent, and actuals are 36 percent complete and 2.3 million spent, so Pipe is 4 points behind and 300 thousand over. Project Meter's latest report is dated 15 June and shows 25 percent complete, where the baseline for 15 June was 30 percent. Before Meter's figures can be added to the program view, one step is missing: ______. Once that step is done, the consolidated view shows each project's variance at 30 June and the program total.
choices: Restate Meter's figures as of 30 June on the same basis as Pipe, instead of treating the 15 June report as if it were current
Show Meter's variance only as a colour rating because its report is older than Pipe's
Average the two projects' percent-complete figures to produce one program percentage before comparing them with the baseline
Round both projects' spend to the nearest 100 thousand so the program total is easier to read
questions.why: Every constituent project must be consolidated with the same date and definitions, so Meter's data has to be brought to 30 June before its variance can be compared fairly with Pipe's.

questions.prompt: In program management, what is a baseline?
choices: A list of the people who will be interviewed about lessons learned at the end of the program
The running total of every invoice paid to suppliers across all projects in the program
The most recent status report written by the program manager before a steering meeting
An agreed reference plan for scope, schedule, cost and expected benefits, fixed at an approved point in time
questions.why: A baseline is the approved reference plan that actual progress is measured against, and it is fixed at a set point in time, which is what the other options fail to describe.

questions.prompt: A telecom upgrade program has four constituent projects. Consolidated spending is 200 thousand under the program budget, but one project, the core routing rebuild, is 25 percent over its own budget and is the prerequisite for a customer-revenue benefit scheduled next quarter. Which consolidated report is most appropriate?
choices: Show each project's variance next to the program total, and flag the routing rebuild overrun along with its effect on the dependent benefit
Report the program as on budget, because the total underspend is larger than the overrun
Remove the routing rebuild from the consolidated view until its overrun is resolved
Report only the percentage of projects that are individually within budget
questions.why: Consolidation must keep each project's variance visible alongside the total, so the overrun and its threat to the benefit are not hidden by the underspend elsewhere.

questions.prompt: A program has two constituent projects. Project Lumen reports percent complete by counting finished tasks, while project Harbor reports percent complete by the share of its budget spent. Both report 50 percent. What should the program do before comparing them against the baseline?
choices: Drop Harbor's figure, since budget-based progress is never valid for consolidation
Restate both projects' progress on one agreed definition, using the same dates and units, before combining them
Use the higher of the two figures as the official program progress
Accept both figures because a 50 percent reading means the same thing for each project
questions.why: Consolidation only produces a fair comparison when every constituent project uses the same definitions, so the two 50 percent figures cannot be combined until they are measured the same way.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says that once each project sends its status, the program status is simply the average of those reports. Explain to them, in your own words, what consolidation should do instead, and name one limit of the consolidated view.
lessons.modelAnswer: Consolidation is not averaging. First, every project reports against the same baseline, dates and units, so the figures can be compared. Then the program team compares each project's actual progress and spend with its planned values and shows each variance separately, because a healthy average can hide one project that is failing. Next, the team checks dependencies, so a problem in an upstream project is shown as a risk to the benefits that depend on it. The result is a status message that says what is off, by how much, what it threatens, and what action is proposed. One limit is that the consolidated view is only as accurate as the project reports feeding it. If projects report optimistic percent complete figures, the program view will look healthy until the problem becomes too large to recover from, so spot checks against the underlying work are still needed.
rubricPoints: Consolidation compares each project's actuals with the same baseline, not a simple average of colours
Each variance in schedule, cost and progress is shown separately so failing projects stay visible
Dependencies between projects are checked so a delay is linked to the benefits it threatens
The status message states the gap, its impact and a proposed corrective action
A limit is named: the view depends on the accuracy of project reports

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a program status situation with conflicting project reports adds the most here, since no listed mission covers program-level reporting.

lessons.plain: When a program is running, you keep comparing what you planned with what is actually happening. The gap between plan and reality is called a variance. Cost variance asks whether you are spending more or less than the budget allows for the work finished so far. Schedule variance asks whether work is finishing earlier or later than planned. Quality and risk variances check whether defects and threats are showing up at a rate or size you did not expect. Once you see a gap, you decide what to change, write that change down as a corrective action, and then check that it works.
lessons.guessPrompt: A program has a total budget of 500,000 and its plan says 100 units of work should be finished by month six. At month six it has finished 60 units and has spent 450,000. Before using any formulas, which gap looks more serious, the spending or the progress? Explain your reasoning in two or three sentences.
lessons.teach:
Three terms carry this idea. Planned value (PV) is the budgeted value of the work the plan says should be finished by a given date. Earned value (EV) is the budgeted value of the work actually finished so far. Actual cost (AC) is what has really been spent. Comparing these three numbers shows whether a program is spending well and moving on time, which is far more useful than asking whether the team seems busy.

Cost variance (CV) equals EV minus AC. A negative number means the program has spent more than the work it has completed is worth. Schedule variance (SV) equals EV minus PV. A negative number means less work is done than the plan required by this date. Two ratios make the same comparison scaled: the cost performance index is EV divided by AC, and the schedule performance index is EV divided by PV. Below 1 is unfavourable.

Worked example. The budget is 500,000 for 100 units, so each unit is worth 5,000. EV is 60 units times 5,000, which gives 300,000. PV is 100 units times 5,000, which gives 500,000. AC is 450,000. CV is 300,000 minus 450,000, which gives negative 150,000. SV is 300,000 minus 500,000, which gives negative 200,000. The cost performance index is 0.67 and the schedule performance index is 0.60. The program is overspent and behind. The corrective action might be a recovery plan that cuts scope or adds resources, with the budget re-baselined only if the sponsor agrees.

Quality and risk use the same discipline. Compare actual defect rates with the planned acceptance threshold, and compare realised risk exposure with the tolerance in the risk register.

The common mistake is treating spending as progress, or reporting a variance without recording a corrective action and its owner. In a multi-project program, a schedule slip in one project pushes the benefits that depend on it later, which can quietly break the business case.

A variance is only useful when it leads to a recorded decision and a follow-up check.

questions.prompt: A data-center migration program has a budget of 800,000 split into 40 work packages, so each package is worth 20,000. At week 10 the plan says 25 packages should be finished, so PV is 500,000. The team has actually finished 18 packages, so EV is 360,000. Actual spending so far is 300,000, so AC is 300,000. CV is EV minus AC, which gives plus 60,000. SV is EV minus PV, which gives 360,000 minus 500,000, or negative 140,000. Step to complete: the schedule performance index (SPI) is the ratio of EV to PV. What is the SPI?
choices: 0.72 (EV divided by PV)
0.28 (SV divided by PV)
0.45 (EV divided by the total budget of 800,000)
1.39 (PV divided by EV)
questions.why: SPI is EV divided by PV, so 360,000 divided by 500,000 gives 0.72, which is below 1 and signals the program is behind schedule.

questions.prompt: A community health program has a budget of 240,000 for 60 units, so each unit is worth 4,000. At month 6 the plan called for 45 units to be finished, and 30 units are actually finished. The program has spent 150,000. What is the cost variance (CV)?
questions.why: CV is EV minus AC; EV is 30 times 4,000, or 120,000, and 120,000 minus 150,000 gives negative 30,000.

questions.prompt: A logistics program reports a cost performance index (CPI) of 0.85 and a schedule performance index (SPI) of 1.10 at its quarterly review. Which reading best matches the variance method?
choices: Favorable on both measures because any ratio above 1 is good and the cost ratio is close to 1
Overspent against completed work and ahead of schedule, so record a cost corrective action with an owner
Underspent because the cost ratio is below 1, so cut resources without a recorded decision
On budget because the schedule ratio is above 1, so no action is needed
questions.why: A CPI below 1 means the spend is higher than the completed work is worth, while an SPI above 1 means the program is ahead; the cost side still needs a recorded corrective action and owner.

questions.prompt: A software rollout program has a defect rate of 4.5 percent against a planned acceptance threshold of 3 percent. Its realised risk exposure is 1.2 million against a risk register tolerance of 900,000. What should the program manager do according to the variance discipline?
choices: Re-baseline the budget immediately so the higher exposure is covered
Record a corrective action with an owner and a follow-up check for both the defect rate and the risk exposure
Accept the defect rate because the rollout is still on time
Treat quality as outside the variance method, so only the risk figure needs action
questions.why: Quality and risk are compared against their own thresholds and tolerances in the same way as cost and schedule, and each variance needs a recorded corrective action, owner, and follow-up check.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would tell whether a program is over budget or behind schedule, and what you would do next. Name one limit of the numbers you would rely on.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would compare three figures: planned value, the budgeted worth of work that should be finished by today; earned value, the budgeted worth of work actually finished; and actual cost, what has really been spent. Earned value minus actual cost tells me whether we are overspent, and earned value minus planned value tells me whether we are behind. If either is negative, I would look at the ratios to judge how serious it is. Then I would record a corrective action with an owner and a date, such as cutting scope, adding resources or re-baselining with the sponsor's approval, and check the next period to see whether the trend improved. One limit is that earned value depends on how fairly work was broken down and valued at the start. If the work packages were poorly sized, the numbers can look precise but mislead, so I would check them against what is physically delivered.
rubricPoints: Defines planned value, earned value and actual cost in plain terms
Computes or explains cost variance and schedule variance with their signs
Links each variance to a recorded corrective action with an owner
Names a real limit of the numbers, such as dependence on work breakdown quality

suggested.rationale: Explaining variances back and naming their limits is the core skill here, and no listed mission or planned engine covers program-level earned value.

lessons.plain: A program is a group of related projects managed together to deliver a business outcome. Along the way things go wrong. A risk is something that might happen later, and an issue is something that has already happened. Managing them well means following the rules agreed in advance, the risk management plan, which says how risks are spotted, scored, owned, and answered. The reason this matters is that the point of a program is the benefit the business receives, such as faster service or lower cost, not just finishing the work. A problem left unmanaged can quietly erode that benefit even when every individual project reports that it is on track.
lessons.guessPrompt: A program has three projects, and the vendor for one of them is two months late. The other two projects are on schedule. Should the program manager act now, and if so, what is the first thing to check?
lessons.teach:
A program is a set of related projects run together so that a business benefit is delivered. A risk is an uncertain event that might affect the program. An issue is a problem that has already happened and needs action now. The risk management plan is the agreed set of rules for handling both: how risks are identified, scored for likelihood and impact, assigned an owner, and answered. A risk register is the running list that records each risk, its score, its owner, its planned response, and its trigger. A trigger is a measurable signal, such as a date passing or a test failing, that tells the team a risk has started to happen. A response is the chosen action: avoid, transfer, mitigate, or accept. Benefits realization means the business actually gets the outcome the program promised, measured after delivery. Why this works: a program manager sees risks across several projects at once, so the program level can act on a threat that no single project team would treat as urgent.

Worked example. A program aims to cut order-processing time by 30 percent. Risk R-07 says the vendor's API sandbox may not be ready by month 5. It is scored likelihood 3 of 5, impact 4 of 5, owner the integration lead, response mitigate by building a test stub, trigger sandbox not delivered by end of month 5. Step one: at month 5 the trigger fires. Step two: the owner logs it in the issue log and confirms the sandbox is late. Step three: the program checks the plan's response, which is to activate the stub. Step four: it compares the forecast benefit date with the program's agreed tolerance. If the slip stays inside tolerance, the team proceeds and records the change. If it breaks tolerance, the issue is escalated to the program board with the benefit impact stated.

Common mistake: updating the risk register every month as a paperwork exercise while ignoring the triggers. Consequence: the benefit date slips without anyone deciding to accept the slip, and the business case that justified funding becomes unreliable.

questions.prompt: A rail operator runs a program of three projects to move ticket sales from paper kiosks to a mobile app, with a target of cutting kiosk maintenance costs by 20 percent. Risk R-12 says the card payment gateway may not receive security certification by month 8. It is scored likelihood 2 of 5, impact 5 of 5, owner the payments workstream lead, response mitigate by running a parallel manual cash reconciliation, and trigger certification not granted by end of month 8. Step 1: at the end of month 8 the certification is still pending, so the trigger fires. Step 2: the payments lead logs it in the issue log and confirms with the certifying body that the decision is late. Step 3: the program checks the plan's response, which is mitigate, so the parallel manual reconciliation is switched on. Step 4: the program compares the forecast slip in the kiosk-cost benefit date, which is 3 weeks, with the agreed tolerance, which is 2 weeks. Step 5: the program must now decide what to do with the slip. What is the correct action for step 5?
choices: Record the slip as within tolerance and carry on with the existing plan unchanged.
Close risk R-12 in the register, since its response has already been activated.
Escalate the issue to the program board with the benefit impact stated, because the slip breaks the agreed tolerance.
Hold the decision until the next monthly register review so that all risks are reviewed together.
questions.why: Once a forecast slip breaks the agreed tolerance, the teaching text says the issue is escalated to the program board with the benefit impact stated, so option C is the only one that follows that rule.

questions.prompt: In a program risk management plan, what is a trigger?
choices: The named person who is accountable for watching a risk and answering it.
A measurable signal, such as a date passing or a test failing, that shows a risk has started to happen.
The product of a risk's likelihood score and its impact score.
The chosen action to avoid, transfer, mitigate or accept a risk.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a trigger as a measurable signal that tells the team a risk has started to happen, which is what option D describes.

questions.prompt: A supplier risk in a retail program is recorded with the trigger supplier has not delivered the test data by 15 March. On 16 March the data is still missing. Which first action matches the program's approach?
choices: Wait for the next monthly update of the risk register before doing anything.
Log the event in the issue log and confirm with the owner that the delivery is late.
Tell the sponsor only after the final benefit date has moved.
Delete the risk from the register because it is no longer a risk.
questions.why: Once a trigger fires, the risk has become an issue that needs action now, so the owner logs it in the issue log and confirms the facts, which is option A.

questions.prompt: A program team updates its risk register every month for paperwork but never checks the triggers between updates. Which consequence does the teaching text warn about?
choices: Risks close automatically on their due dates, so no one tracks them any more.
The program underspends its budget because contingency funds are never released.
The risk register becomes too long to read and has to be split into two registers.
The benefit date slips without anyone deciding to accept the slip, and the business case becomes unreliable.
questions.why: The teaching text states that ignoring triggers lets the benefit date slip without a decision to accept it, which makes the business case that justified funding unreliable, matching option C.

lessons.explainPrompt: A sponsor asks why you are spending time on a risk that the project teams describe as a small schedule issue. Explain to a teammate how you would decide whether it is a program-level issue, what the risk management plan tells you to do, and which limit or tradeoff you must watch so the expected benefit is protected.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by checking the risk register and the trigger for that risk. If the trigger has fired, it is no longer just a project concern, it is a program issue, because it can move the benefit date. I would confirm the facts with the owner, then follow the response already in the plan, such as activating a fallback. Next I would compare the forecast benefit date with the tolerance the program agreed. If the slip stays within tolerance, I record it and keep watching. If it breaks tolerance, I escalate to the program board with the effect on the benefit, not just the effect on the schedule. The tradeoff to watch is that escalating too early wastes governance time, while escalating too late means the business finds out after the benefit is already lost.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes a risk from an issue and says a fired trigger turns a risk into an issue to act on
Refers to the risk management plan, the risk register, the owner, and the planned response
Compares the forecast benefit date against the agreed tolerance before deciding to escalate
Names a limit or tradeoff, such as escalating too early versus too late

suggested.rationale: No listed OpsForge mission or planned engine practices program-level risk handling, so explaining the reasoning back is the core skill here.

lessons.plain: When a program is ending, stopping the work is not enough. A program is a group of related projects run together to deliver a business outcome. Closing it well means three things: formally signing off each project that made up the program, handing the working results to the people who will run them day to day, and saving what the team learned so the next program starts smarter. Think of finishing a house renovation. You check each room is done, hand over keys and manuals to the occupants, and file the plans and lessons for the next renovation.
lessons.guessPrompt: A program has five projects. Four have been formally closed, but the fifth project's team says their work is finished and they have disbanded. What is the most important step still missing before the program can close, and why?
lessons.teach:
Program closure is the formal end of a program. It has three parts. First, constituent-project closeout approval. A constituent project is one of the separate projects the program coordinates. Each one must be formally closed, with its deliverables accepted, its final cost and schedule recorded, and its open issues resolved or assigned to someone. The program sponsor, the executive accountable for the program, signs off each closeout, so a project is never closed just because its team went quiet. Second, transition to operations. A transition is the handover of the delivered capability to the business unit or support group that will run it after the program leaves. It is a named, documented handover with owners, runbooks (step-by-step operating guides), support arrangements and a dated acceptance. Third, archiving lessons learned. Lessons learned are recorded observations about what worked and what did not, captured during the program and reviewed at closure. They go into a retrievable archive so future programs can use them.

Why this matters: a program's value is usually realized after it ends, when the outputs are used and the benefits appear. If nobody owns the outputs after closure, the benefits quietly decay.

Worked example. A program delivers a new customer portal through three projects. Step 1: the portal project's closeout is checked against its acceptance criteria, remaining defects are logged and assigned to the support team, and the sponsor signs the closeout. Step 2: the operations manager accepts the handover, receives the support runbook and the on-call schedule, and a dated acceptance is recorded. Step 3: the lessons from all three projects are reviewed and filed in the program archive, including a note that vendor onboarding ran two weeks late.

Common mistake: treating closure as a celebration after the final sprint, with no sponsor sign-off and no named operations owner. Consequence: when an incident hits the portal six months later, nobody has the authority or documentation to fix it, and the lessons that would have prevented it are lost.

A closed program is only finished when each project is formally approved, the outputs have a named owner in operations, and the lessons are stored where the next program can find them.

questions.prompt: A city transit authority runs a program to replace its ticketing system through two constituent projects: a card-reader hardware project and a fare-engine project. Step 1: The card-reader project's closeout is checked against its acceptance criteria, its final cost and schedule are recorded, and its two open defects are assigned to the field maintenance team. The program sponsor signs that closeout. Step 2: The fare-engine project's open issues are resolved, its closeout is checked the same way, and the sponsor signs it. Step 3: The transit operations manager accepts the handover of both systems, receives the runbooks and support arrangements, and a dated acceptance is recorded. Step 4: The lessons from both projects are reviewed at closure. What remains to finish program closure?
choices: Hold the program open until the card-reader vendor's warranty period ends
Ask the sponsor to re-sign both closeouts after the transit team's annual budget review
Store the lessons learned in a retrievable program archive so future programs can use them
Transfer the unspent program budget to the next program without writing up the lessons
questions.why: Program closure has three parts, and the archiving of lessons learned into a retrievable archive is the third one still missing after the closeouts and the operations handover are done.

questions.prompt: A hospital network's program has a constituent project whose team stopped reporting after final testing. The program manager proposes marking that project closed because nobody is working on it anymore. Under the closure approach described in the course, what is the required next step?
choices: Hold it open until the program sponsor reviews and signs a closeout that confirms accepted deliverables and records the final cost and schedule
Ask the hospital's finance office to confirm the budget is spent
Delete its open issues so the closeout looks clean
Mark it closed and move the team to the next program
questions.why: A constituent project must be formally approved by the program sponsor with its deliverables accepted and its final cost and schedule recorded, and a team going quiet does not count as closure.

questions.prompt: A university's program delivered a new timetabling system. Six weeks after closure, a scheduling fault appears and staff cannot find who owns the system or how to restart its scheduler. Which gap in closure most directly explains this?
choices: The lessons learned were not written in the program archive
The program did not record a dated, named handover to an operations owner with runbooks and support arrangements
The program's constituent projects were too many to track
The sponsor signed the closeout before the vendor invoice arrived
questions.why: Transition to operations requires a named, documented handover with owners, runbooks, support arrangements and a dated acceptance, and without it nobody has clear authority or documentation to fix a live fault.

questions.prompt: A retail chain's program had two projects that slipped. Which of these items is a lesson learned as the course defines it, suitable for filing in the program archive at closure?
choices: The sponsor's signature on the closeout form
The list of store locations that received the new system first
A recorded observation that the payment gateway vendor delivered four weeks late because the contract did not specify test-environment access, so future programs should check this before signing
The final invoice total for the store fixtures
questions.why: A lesson learned is a recorded observation about what worked or did not work, and the vendor delay with its cause is that kind of observation, while the other items are closeout records or outputs rather than lessons.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has just joined the program office why closing a program takes more than shutting down the project teams. Name one limit or tradeoff that the closure process can run into.
lessons.modelAnswer: Shutting down the teams stops the spending, but it does not secure the program's value. Closure needs three things. Each constituent project needs a formal closeout approved by the sponsor, confirming its deliverables were accepted and its open items were assigned. The delivered capability needs a named transition to the operations group, with runbooks, support ownership and an accepted date, because benefits only appear while someone runs the outputs. Lessons learned from all the projects should be filed in a searchable archive. The tradeoff is time and attention. A thorough closure competes with the team's move to new work, and sponsors are often slow to sign off, so the program office should schedule the sign-offs early and agree the handover criteria before the final sprint rather than after it.
rubricPoints: Closure requires a formal sponsor-approved closeout for each constituent project, not just team shutdown
Transition to operations means a named, documented handover with an accepted owner so benefits continue
Lessons learned must be captured and archived in a retrievable form for future programs
Names a real limit, such as time pressure or slow sponsor sign-off, and how to plan around it

suggested.rationale: Explaining closure back to a teammate, including its tradeoffs, is the core skill here, and no listed mission or planned engine covers program closure directly.

lessons.plain: A benefits realization plan is a written plan that says what good result a program is meant to produce, how that result will be measured, who is responsible for it, and when it should show up. Think of a city building a new bus route: the route is the project, but the goal is that more people get to work faster. The plan answers how anyone will know that happened. Before any change starts, you record where things stand today, so you can later prove what moved. Then you show the plan to the sponsor, the person who funds the program and is accountable for its value, and get their agreement.
lessons.guessPrompt: A program will reduce warehouse order errors. Before anything changes, what single number would you record first, and why might a sponsor later doubt the result if you had not recorded it?
lessons.teach:
A benefit is a measurable improvement that matters to the organization, such as faster claim payments or lower cost per order. A benefits realization plan sets out how the program will create these benefits, when they should appear, and who owns them. Its measurement criteria are the rules for judging success. For each benefit they name the metric (what is counted), the baseline (its value before the program changes anything), the target (the value to reach), the data source and method, the owner, and how often it is reviewed. This works because a benefit you cannot measure cannot be argued about, and a target without a baseline is only a guess about how far things moved.

Worked example. A program aims to shorten insurance claim payment time. Step 1: define the metric as the average number of calendar days from claim submission to payment. Step 2: pull three months of claims data before any change, giving a baseline of 12 days. Step 3: set a target of 6 days, to be reached six months after the final project closes. Step 4: name the claims operations director as owner, the claims system as the data source, and monthly review. Step 5: write this up and present it to the sponsor, who approves it. Now the plan can be checked against real numbers later.

Common mistake: taking the baseline after work has begun, when early changes have already moved the number, so the program cannot show what it caused. Consequence: when results arrive, nobody can tell whether the gain came from the program, a seasonal dip, or an unrelated change, and the sponsor loses confidence in the benefits claimed.

A baseline is only useful if it is captured before the first change and the measurement rules are agreed in advance.

questions.prompt: A distribution depot wants to shorten the time trucks spend between gate-in and gate-out. Step 1: define the metric as the average minutes from gate-in to gate-out per truck visit. Step 2 is missing from this trace. Step 3: set the target at 50 minutes, to be reached three months after the gate-scheduling pilot closes. Step 4: name the depot operations manager as owner, the gate terminal log as data source, and weekly review. What belongs in Step 2?
choices: Pull four weeks of gate terminal records from before the pilot starts, giving a baseline of 74 minutes.
Ask drivers for their estimate of a typical wait and record it as the baseline, about 60 minutes.
Set the baseline equal to the 50-minute target so the sponsor sees one clear goal.
Start the gate-scheduling pilot and record the first two weeks of averages as the baseline, which comes to 61 minutes.
questions.why: The baseline must be captured from data gathered before any change, using the agreed metric, so the later result can be compared against an untouched starting value.

questions.prompt: A regional water utility wants to cut the average time from a customer leak report to crew arrival. Which choice correctly identifies the baseline?
choices: The crew arrival time recorded in the four weeks before the new dispatch tool is switched on, averaged from the work order system.
The 4-hour response time the utility publishes for customers, since it defines what is acceptable.
The average crew arrival time measured in the first month after the dispatch tool goes live.
The number of leak reports received each month, since that is the figure the program will change.
questions.why: A baseline is the value of the metric before the program changes anything, taken from the agreed data source, so only the pre-change weeks qualify.

questions.prompt: A program team sets its benefit target only after the first month of results come in, choosing a figure that looks achievable. Which problem does this most directly create?
choices: The data source must be replaced because a numeric target cannot be stored in the same system.
The target is no longer a fixed rule for judging success, so the result cannot be tested against a standard agreed in advance.
The sponsor will reject any target that is set later than the original project plan.
The metric can no longer be reviewed monthly, because targets are only allowed to be reviewed annually.
questions.why: Measurement criteria are supposed to be agreed before data arrives; a target chosen after seeing results can be bent to fit whatever happened, so it proves nothing.

questions.prompt: A sponsor asks the team to add a second metric for an existing benefit after data collection has already started. What is the best response under the plan's rules?
choices: Replace the original metric so the team only reports one number to the sponsor.
Decline the request, because measurement criteria cannot be discussed once the plan is approved.
Add the metric quietly and back-date its baseline to the first week of collection.
Check whether pre-change data exists for the new metric, then present the addition as a proposed change to the agreed criteria for sponsor approval, flagging any missing baseline.
questions.why: Changes to measurement criteria go to the sponsor for approval, and any baseline that was not captured before the change must be openly flagged rather than invented.

lessons.explainPrompt: You are presenting a benefits realization plan to a sponsor who asks how anyone will know the program worked. In your own words, explain which measurement criteria you would include, why the baseline must be captured before the work starts, and one limit or tradeoff of measuring benefits this way.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would tell the sponsor that each benefit has a named metric, a baseline measured before any change, a target with a date, a data source, an owner, and a review schedule. For claim payment time, for example, the baseline is the average days from submission to payment over the last three months, and the target is a specific reduction after the program closes. The baseline has to come first because otherwise early changes distort the starting point and we cannot separate the program's effect from seasonal or unrelated trends. The main limit is that some benefits take a year or more to appear, and some depend on things outside the program, such as market conditions or staff behavior. So the plan should say which results the program can directly influence and which need shared accountability with operations.
rubricPoints: Each benefit has a metric, baseline, target, data source, owner and review frequency
The baseline is captured before any change so the effect of the program can be isolated
Targets are tied to a date, often after the program closes, not just to delivery
A real limit is named, such as delayed benefits or outside factors that the program cannot control

suggested.rationale: Applying the plan to a messy sponsor scenario, with a baseline and measures to choose, teaches this objective better than any existing OpsForge mission, none of which covers benefits.

lessons.plain: When several projects inside one larger program run at the same time, they often overlap. Two teams may need the same data feed, one new system may replace three old ones, or one training session may serve several projects at once. Spotting these overlaps is finding synergies, where combined effort produces more value than the separate parts, and efficiencies, where the same result costs less money, time, or effort. The program's plan for how benefits will be delivered then gets updated to reflect these shortcuts, instead of staying frozen at the original estimate.
lessons.guessPrompt: Two projects in one program each plan to buy a separate reporting tool, with separate budgets and separate contracts. What is the most useful thing the program manager could do, and what would change in the benefits plan as a result?
lessons.teach:
A synergy is a combined result that is larger than the sum of the separate projects' results. An efficiency is the same outcome reached with less money, time, or effort. Both are found by looking across the whole program rather than inside one component project, because overlaps are invisible to a team that only sees its own scope. The benefits realization plan is the program's document describing which benefits will be delivered, how each will be measured, when, and by whom. It is the baseline against which progress is judged, so when a synergy changes the picture, the plan has to change with it.

Why it works: component projects often share inputs such as data, vendors, staff, and infrastructure, and share outputs such as customers and processes. When the program maps these shared elements across the life cycle, duplicate work can be removed and one delivery can satisfy several benefits at once.

Worked example: Project A builds a customer portal and budgets 400 thousand for a data feed. Project B needs the same feed and budgets 350 thousand. Project C plans a dashboard that depends on the feed. Step 1: the program manager lists shared dependencies and finds all three need the feed. Step 2: the feed is built once under Project A, so the 350 thousand planned by Project B is removed from the budget. Step 3: the benefit 'reduced time to answer customer queries' now depends on the shared feed, so its target date is re-checked and the cost-saving benefit records the avoided 350 thousand. Step 4: the plan is updated, the change is logged, and sponsors receive the new baseline.

Common mistake: counting the same synergy as a benefit in two projects, or claiming savings without reducing the original budget line. Another frequent error is updating the cost figure but leaving dependent dates and measures unchanged.

Consequence: if the plan is not updated, the program still reports the duplicate budget as needed, sponsors see false variance, and teams keep building the same feed.

questions.prompt: A city transit agency runs three linked projects. Project Q installs a vehicle location tracking system and budgets 220 thousand for a map data licence. Project R needs the same licence and budgets 180 thousand for it. Project S builds a delay dashboard that cannot work without the licence. The program manager follows this worked sequence. Step 1: lists the shared dependency and finds that Q, R and S all need the same licence. Step 2: the licence is bought once under Project Q, so the 180 thousand in Project R's budget is removed. Step 3 is missing from this text and must be filled in before the sequence is complete. Step 4: the plan is updated, the change is logged, and sponsors receive the new baseline. Which action fills Step 3?
choices: Keep Project R's 180 thousand in the budget and label it as a contingency reserve
Leave the delay reduction target and its measure unchanged, because only the cost line moved
Re-check the benefit dates and measures that depend on the shared licence, and record the 180 thousand as avoided cost in the benefits realization plan
Count the 180 thousand as a saving in the benefit registers of both Project R and Project S
questions.why: Step 3 in the teaching pattern re-checks the dependent benefits and records the avoided cost, so the plan reflects the synergy consistently, while the other choices repeat the listed common mistakes of double counting, leaving dependent measures unchanged, or keeping the duplicate budget.

questions.prompt: A water utility has two projects. One replaces pipe sensors and the other upgrades its billing system. Both would be cheaper if they shared one network connection, and combining them lets the utility deliver the same service with less spending. Which label best describes this result, and what is the correct first move?
choices: An efficiency, so the program should cut the shared connection budget line and update the realization plan to show the same outcome at lower cost
An efficiency, so the program should wait until both projects close before reviewing the connection
A synergy, so the program should add the two benefits together to report a larger total
A synergy, so the program should keep both connection budgets because combined results cannot be measured
questions.why: Same outcome with less money is an efficiency, and the teaching text says the duplicate budget must come out and the plan must be updated accordingly, so the other options misdefine the term or skip the required update.

questions.prompt: A hospital network runs a staff scheduling project and a credentialing project. Both separately buy the same 45 thousand training course for nursing staff, and the credentialing project's plan also counts the course's completion rate as its own benefit. A program manager finds the overlap. Which action best matches what the teaching text calls for?
choices: Keep both purchases and report the completion rate as a benefit in both projects to show strong results
Buy the course once, remove the duplicate budget line, and reassign the completion benefit so it is recorded in only one place in the realization plan
Remove the course from both projects and report the saving as an efficiency without changing any benefit entries
Ask the sponsor to approve a new benefit for training so that both projects can keep their own version
questions.why: The teaching text warns against counting the same synergy as a benefit in two projects and against claiming savings without reducing the original budget line, so buying once, removing the duplicate line and keeping one benefit entry is the correct response.

questions.prompt: A regional airline's program had a fuel-logging project and a maintenance scheduling project sharing one inspection data feed. The fuel-logging team cut the feed's budget after the shared build was consolidated, but the realization plan still shows the original target date for maintenance cost reduction and the original measure of inspections per month, both based on the old separate builds. What is the consequence the teaching text predicts for this program?
choices: The program still reports a duplicate need, sponsors see false variance against stale dates and measures, and teams may keep building parallel feeds
The program will exceed its maintenance target because the shared feed produces better data by default
The program will automatically update the dependent dates once the budget changes, so no further action is needed
The program will report the cost saving as early, which means sponsors will see no variance at all
questions.why: The teaching text says that updating the cost figure while leaving dependent dates and measures unchanged leads to false variance and continued duplicate building, which is the consequence described for an unupdated plan.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would find synergies across the program's projects and what you would change in the benefits realization plan when you find one. Name one limit or tradeoff of counting a synergy as a benefit.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by listing each project's shared inputs and outputs, such as data feeds, vendors, staff, and infrastructure, and mark where two or more projects depend on the same thing. Then I would check the life cycle timeline to see which shared work happens first, because building it once early usually saves the most. When I find a real overlap, I update the benefits realization plan: I move the shared cost to one owner, reduce the duplicate budget line, adjust the target dates of benefits that depend on the shared work, and record the change so sponsors can see the new baseline. The main tradeoff is that a synergy depends on the shared item being delivered on time. If the owning project slips, every benefit that depends on it slips too, so I link those benefits to a named dependency and watch it closely rather than presenting the savings as certain.
rubricPoints: Identifies shared inputs, outputs, or dependencies across projects in the program
Distinguishes a synergy (combined value) from an efficiency (same result with less cost or effort)
Updates the benefits realization plan: costs, target dates, and measures tied to the shared work
Records the change and communicates the new baseline to sponsors
Names a limit such as dependence on the owning project's delivery or the risk of double-counting

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers program-level benefits planning, so reading the teaching text followed by the explanation exercise is the best fit.

lessons.plain: A sustainment plan is the written plan for keeping a program's benefits alive after the program's projects have closed. A program is a group of related projects run to deliver a business outcome, such as faster customer billing or fewer service outages. Once the program ends, the new way of working belongs to the operations people who run it. Without a plan, nobody is assigned to watch the results, the measurements stop, and the gains slowly slip back. The plan names who owns each benefit afterwards, which measures show it is still happening, how often they are checked, and which tools collect the data. It works like a car handed over with a service schedule, a named mechanic and a dashboard warning light, rather than just handing over the keys.
lessons.guessPrompt: A program closes and its new process is handed to the operations team. Six months later the promised savings have quietly disappeared, even though the project was marked successful. What is the most likely reason, and what single item would have prevented it?
lessons.teach:
A sustainment plan sets out how a benefit keeps being delivered after the program's projects are closed. A benefit is a measurable gain the business expects, such as fewer invoice errors or a lower cost per service call. Sustainment means keeping that gain in place over time. The plan has three parts. Processes say who runs the new way of working and who is accountable for each benefit after handover. Metrics are the specific measures, each with a baseline (the value before the change), a target (the value you want), and a threshold (the level that triggers a review). Tools are the reports, dashboards and review forums used to collect the numbers and make decisions.

It works because a benefit is only real while someone measures it and acts when it drops. Program teams disband, so the plan transfers that watching duty to a permanent owner before closure.

Worked example: a billing change has a baseline invoice error rate of 8 percent and a target of 2 percent. The plan names the billing operations manager as owner, sets a monthly metric pulled from the billing system, and sets a threshold of 3 percent. In month four the rate reads 3.4 percent, which crosses the threshold. The owner raises it at the monthly operations review, finds that new staff were never trained on the revised form, arranges training, and the rate returns to 2.1 percent within two cycles.

Common mistake: copying the project closing report into a sustainment plan without naming an owner, a measure or a review date. Then nobody sees the drop.

Consequence: the reporting job was set up under the project budget, so it stops when the project closes, and the error rate climbs for months before anyone notices.

A sustainment plan without a named owner, a measured baseline and a review trigger is not a working plan, because the benefit will erode unseen.

questions.prompt: A regional food distributor has a sustainment plan for a new picking route, meaning the fixed order in which staff collect items for customer orders. Its measure is the on-time pick rate, the share of orders picked by the daily cut-off time. The baseline (the value before the change) was 81 percent, and the target (the value wanted) is 95 percent. The plan names the warehouse shift lead as owner, pulls a weekly metric from the warehouse system, and sets a threshold (the level that triggers a review) of 88 percent. In week six the rate reads 86.5 percent, which is below the threshold. The shift lead raises it at the weekly stand-up and finds that agency staff were never shown the new route. Which step completes the sequence?
choices: The shift lead arranges a briefing for agency staff on the new route, then re-measures the weekly rate until it recovers toward the target.
The baseline is reset to 86.5 percent so the new figure becomes the starting point.
The program team closes the sustainment plan, since the threshold has now been reported.
The target is lowered to 86 percent so that the reading counts as on track.
questions.why: The owner acts on the cause found at review and then checks the metric against the target, which is how the plan keeps the benefit in place, whereas the other options either end the watch or change the measures to hide the drop.

questions.prompt: A university IT help desk cut its ticket reopen rate (the share of closed tickets that customers reopen) from 14 percent to 5 percent. The team sets a review trigger at 8 percent. In a sustainment plan, what is the 8 percent figure called?
choices: The threshold, because it is the level that triggers a review.
The tool, because it is the report used to see the reopen rate.
The baseline, because it is the level the team measured after the change.
The target, because it is the value the team wants to reach.
questions.why: A threshold is the level that triggers a review, which is what the 8 percent does here, while the baseline is the pre-change value and the target is the desired value.

questions.prompt: A city transit authority wants bus on-time running to last after its improvement project closes. Its plan names the depot supervisor as owner and a weekly on-time metric with a baseline of 71 percent and a target of 90 percent. However, the weekly reporting job is paid for from the project budget and no review date is set. What is the most serious flaw in this plan?
choices: The threshold should equal the target so that every miss triggers a review.
The baseline should have been taken after closure, when the figures are settled.
The target of 90 percent is too ambitious for a 71 percent baseline.
The reporting job depends on the project budget and stops at closure, so a drop in on-time running would go unseen.
