questions.why: A benefit is only real while someone measures it, and a reporting job that ends with the project means nobody sees the erosion, which is the failure the plan is meant to prevent.

questions.prompt: A bank's card dispute program has a sustainment plan with these items: the average days to resolve a dispute, measured monthly; the head of card operations, accountable for the figure; a 10-day level that prompts a review; and a monthly dispute dashboard reviewed at the operations forum. Which item is a tool?
choices: The average days to resolve a dispute, measured monthly.
The head of card operations, accountable for the figure.
A 10-day level that prompts a review.
A monthly dispute dashboard reviewed at the operations forum.
questions.why: Tools are the reports, dashboards and review forums used to collect the numbers and make decisions, so the dashboard reviewed at a forum is the tool, while the measured days is the metric and the 10-day level is the threshold.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a sustainment plan must contain so that benefits continue after the program closes, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on it.
lessons.modelAnswer: A sustainment plan turns the benefits into something operations keeps running after the program team leaves. For each benefit it names a permanent owner, a metric with a baseline and target, a threshold that triggers a review, the data source, the review cadence and the forum where decisions are made. The main limit is that the plan only protects what someone is funded and motivated to watch. If the owner's budget is cut or the reporting tool belongs to the project, the measures stop and the benefit erodes without any alarm. A second tradeoff is that tight thresholds create noise and many reviews, while loose ones let a slow decline go unnoticed for months. So the plan should be checked at handover, and its owner should confirm that the metrics still run.
rubricPoints: Names a permanent owner for each benefit after handover
Defines metrics with a baseline, a target and a review threshold
Specifies the tools, data sources and review cadence used to monitor
Notes a limit such as lost funding, tool ownership or threshold tradeoffs

suggested.rationale: Explaining what a sustainment plan must contain and its limits back to a teammate is the core skill here, and no listed mission covers benefits sustainment.

lessons.plain: A benefit is a result the program is meant to produce for the organisation, such as faster invoice payment or lower costs, and it is tracked with numbers. Monitoring means checking those numbers regularly against the plan. Variance analysis asks how far the actual result differs from the planned result and why. Forecasting predicts where the number will end up if nothing changes. What-if scenarios test how that prediction would shift under different assumptions. Corrective action is the step you take when the forecast says a benefit is at risk, such as changing a process, reassigning people, or asking the sponsor to approve a different plan. The goal is to protect the benefit, not just to report that it is slipping.
lessons.guessPrompt: A program aims to cut invoice processing from 10 days to 4 days by the end of the year. At month 6 the average is 8.5 days, but the plan said 7. What is the most useful next step, and why is simply reporting the miss not enough?
lessons.teach: A benefit is a measurable outcome the business expects after the program delivers its outputs. Each benefit has a metric, a baseline (the value before the program started), and a planned target with a planned path over time. Monitoring compares actual values with that planned path. Variance is the difference between actual and planned. An actual of 8.5 days against a plan of 7 days is a variance of plus 1.5 days, which is worse here because lower is better. Variance analysis asks why the gap exists and whether it is a one-off spike or a trend. A forecast projects the metric forward from recent actuals. A what-if scenario changes one assumption, such as a tool go-live date or a monthly improvement rate, and shows the effect on the forecast so options can be compared before committing. Worked example: the baseline is 10 days and the month-12 target is 4 days. At month 6 the actual is 8.5 days, a variance of plus 1.5 days. The last three months improved by about 0.3 days per month, so at that rate month 12 lands near 6.7 days, well short of 4. A what-if in which the new tool doubles the monthly improvement to 0.6 days gives about 4.9 days at month 12, still short. Corrective action: find the root cause (missing purchase-order data causing rework), add an intake check, bring the tool forward if feasible, update the benefits register with the revised forecast, and take it to the sponsor for a decision. Common mistake: reporting a variance without a cause, a forecast, or an action, or quietly moving the target to hide the shortfall. Target changes need sponsor approval and must be recorded. Consequence: if the shortfall is hidden, the funding case rests on a number the business will not see, and operations inherits a lower result than promised. Corrective action protects realization only when it is specific, owned and reflected in the register.

questions.prompt: A city transit authority aims to cut the average time to process a fare refund, measured in days, from a baseline of 14 days to a month-9 target of 5 days. The planned path is a straight line, so the plan drops by 1 day per month. At month 4 the actual is 11 days. Step 1: the planned value at month 4 is 10 days (14 minus 4). Step 2: the variance is plus 1 day, which is worse because lower is better. Step 3: the last three months improved by about 0.2 days per month, so a forecast from recent actuals puts month 9 near 10 days, 5 days short of target. Which is the missing step 4 that protects realization?
choices: Report the program as on track, since the variance is only 1 day.
Record the root cause, the forecast and the planned action in the benefits register, and take the shortfall to the sponsor for a decision.
Move the month-9 target up to 10 days so that it matches the forecast.
Wait until month 9 to see whether the gap closes on its own.
questions.why: A variance needs a cause, a forecast and an owned action reflected in the register, and any shortfall beyond the target goes to the sponsor, not into a quiet target change or a wait.

questions.prompt: A hospital scheduling program tracks average patient wait for a clinic appointment. The baseline is 180 minutes, and the planned path at month 4 is 150 minutes. The actual at month 4 is 162 minutes. Which statement describes the variance correctly?
choices: A variance of plus 12 minutes, which is unfavourable because lower is better.
A variance of plus 12 minutes, which is favourable because the number went up.
A variance of minus 12 minutes, which is unfavourable because the number went down.
A variance of minus 12 minutes, which is favourable.
questions.why: Variance is actual minus planned, giving plus 12 minutes, and since waiting time should fall, a rise is unfavourable.

questions.prompt: A warehouse program tracks picking errors per 1,000 orders. A team member runs a what-if scenario that changes both the software go-live date and the monthly improvement rate at the same time, then reports that the forecast at month 12 is acceptable. What is the main weakness of this analysis?
choices: The forecast should use a straight-line plan instead of recent actuals.
The scenario changed two assumptions, so the effect of each cannot be separated and options cannot be compared cleanly.
The scenario should not be compared with the baseline at all.
The month-12 result should be ignored because only the final month matters.
questions.why: A what-if is meant to change one assumption at a time so that its effect on the forecast can be seen and options compared fairly.

questions.prompt: A finance program has a benefit of reducing average invoice payment time from 30 days. After a shortfall, a program manager raises the target to 38 days without asking the sponsor and updates only the target field in the register. What should the program manager do next?
choices: Keep the 38-day target because it is achievable and the business will see a better result.
Escalate to the sponsor, obtain approval for the target change, and record the change in the register alongside the original target.
Remove the invoice payment benefit from the register so that the shortfall no longer appears.
Leave the register unchanged and mention the revised target only in the next status meeting.
questions.why: Target changes need sponsor approval and must be recorded with the original value visible, so the shortfall is not hidden.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would tell whether a benefit is on track, what you would do if it is not, and what limits your forecast.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would compare the actual metric with the planned path at the same point in time, which gives the variance, and I would check whether it is a single spike or a sustained trend. If the trend is adverse, I would forecast the end-of-program value by extending recent actuals, then run one or two what-if scenarios on the assumptions I can change, such as a go-live date or the improvement rate. If the forecast still misses the target, I would find the root cause, agree a corrective action with a named owner and a date, update the benefits register, and take the revised forecast to the sponsor for a decision rather than changing the target myself. The limit is that a forecast built from a few months of trend is only as good as the stability of the process behind it, so I would state my confidence in the number and set a date to re-forecast.
rubricPoints: Defines variance as actual minus planned, compared at the same point in time on the planned path.
Distinguishes a one-off spike from a sustained trend before forecasting.
Names a corrective action with an owner and date, and records it in the benefits register.
States that target changes need sponsor approval and that forecasts have limits.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a variance, forecast and what-if situation adds the most here, and no listed mission covers benefits metrics.

lessons.plain: When a big program is made of smaller projects, each smaller project eventually finishes. Finishing is not the same as the program getting its promised value. This objective is about checking, before a smaller project is signed off, that what it hands over really lets the value happen: the things it built are working, the people who will run them have accepted them, and the measures used to prove the benefit are in place. If the checks pass, the project closes. If they fall short, the gaps are recorded and fixed or accepted by the sponsor first.
lessons.guessPrompt: A program has three projects building a new dispatch system. Project 2 finishes on time and under budget, with every planned feature delivered. Should the program count the benefit that depends on Project 2 as secured? What would you check first?
lessons.teach: A constituent project is one of the smaller projects grouped inside a program to deliver a shared outcome. Closure means the project formally ends once its scope is complete. Transition is the handover of what the project built to the people or teams who will run it day to day, often called operations. A benefit is a measurable improvement the organisation cares about, and benefit-realization criteria are the agreed tests that say when that improvement is actually happening, such as a target response time sustained over a set period. Why verify before closing? A project can deliver every feature and still leave the benefit out of reach, because the benefit depends on operations using the output, on the right measurement being live, and on someone owning it afterwards. Verification means comparing the project's closure evidence against those criteria in the benefits realization plan, and confirming that the operations owner has formally accepted the handover. Worked example: Project 2 builds a new vehicle-location feed. Step 1: the criteria say the dispatch-delay benefit requires the feed live in every depot and a delay dashboard reporting for eight weeks. Step 2: closure evidence shows the feed live in five of six depots. Step 3: the dashboard exists but has no named owner. Step 4: the program records the gap in the benefits register, keeps the project open until the sixth depot is live and an owner is named, and re-checks before closing. Common mistake: treating a completed scope list as proof of benefit. Consequence in a running system: if the project closes early, nobody watches the dashboard, delays rise unnoticed, and the forecast benefit quietly disappears. Closure is complete only when the benefit path is confirmed.

questions.prompt: A retailer's program builds a shared picking tool, a handheld app that guides warehouse staff to items, for two distribution centres. The program's benefits register (the log where each benefit, its criteria and its status are recorded) says the benefit is confirmed only when pick accuracy stays above 99.5 percent for six weeks at both centres and a named site manager owns the accuracy report. Step 1: the criteria require six weeks above 99.5 percent at both centres with a named owner. Step 2: closure evidence shows the tool live at both centres and accuracy at 99.7 percent for the first four weeks, with the site manager named as owner. Step 3: [missing; you supply it]. Step 4: the program closes the project only after the sixth week confirms the target at both centres and the owner has accepted the handover. What is the missing Step 3?
choices: Record in the benefits register that the criteria need six weeks but only four are evidenced, and keep the project open until the sixth week is confirmed.
Ask the tool vendor to lower the accuracy target to 99.7 percent so the four weeks count as passing.
Mark the benefit as realised in the register, since accuracy is already above target and the owner is in place.
Accept the handover and close the project, because the tool is live at both centres and the scope is complete.
questions.why: The correct step records the gap against the agreed criteria and keeps the project open, which is how verification works when the evidence is short of the criteria.

questions.prompt: In this course, what are benefit-realization criteria?
choices: The agreed tests that show when a measurable improvement is actually happening, such as a target sustained over a set period.
A list of the constituent projects that must each finish on schedule.
The final budget figure the sponsor approved for the program.
The contract clauses that define how a vendor is paid after handover.
questions.why: The teaching text defines benefit-realization criteria as the agreed tests that say when a measurable improvement is actually happening, with a sustained target as the example.

questions.prompt: A smaller project inside a hospital-scheduling program has completed all its scope. The clinic operations manager has not yet signed the handover, and no one has been named to run the no-show report the benefit depends on. What should the program do before closing this project?
choices: Reduce the no-show target so the current report can pass without an owner.
Close the project now, since scope completion is the only formal requirement for closure.
Hold closure, note the open handover and missing report owner in the benefits register, and re-check before closing.
Transfer the no-show report to the sponsor's office and close the project the same week.
questions.why: Verification requires confirming the operations owner has accepted the handover and that the measurement is owned, so the project stays open and the gap is recorded until both are in place.

questions.prompt: A logistics program's constituent project delivers a new route-planning tool. The sponsor accepts the completed deliverables and the project is closed, but nobody checks the fuel-cost benefit criteria afterwards. What is the most likely consequence in the running system?
choices: Fuel costs fall further than forecast because the tool is already live.
Fuel costs rise unnoticed and the forecast benefit quietly disappears, because nobody is watching the measure.
The tool is repaired by the vendor during routine support, so the benefit is kept.
The program automatically reopens the project when costs drift.
questions.why: Closing on completed deliverables without checking the benefit path means no one monitors the measure, so the forecast benefit can erode without anyone noticing.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a constituent project should not be formally closed just because its deliverables are complete, and name one limit or tradeoff of holding it open.
lessons.modelAnswer: Completed deliverables only prove the project built what it promised. The benefit depends on that output being handed over and used, measured against the agreed criteria in the benefits realization plan. So before closure I check the closure evidence against those criteria, confirm operations has formally accepted the handover, and check that measurement is live with a named owner. If a gap exists, I record it in the benefits register and either keep the project open or have the sponsor accept the risk in writing. The tradeoff is real: holding a project open delays closure, ties up staff and budget, and can make a finished team look unproductive. Sometimes a sponsor will accept a partial transition with a dated plan, but that acceptance has to be explicit and tracked, not assumed. Otherwise the benefit fades once the program team has moved on.
rubricPoints: Closure is judged against benefit-realization criteria, not only scope completion.
Transition needs formal acceptance by the operations owner, and measurement needs a named owner.
Gaps are recorded in the benefits register and either resolved or explicitly accepted by the sponsor.
Names the tradeoff of delaying closure against cost and team time.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers benefits closure, so a reasoning scenario best tests the verification judgement.

lessons.plain: A benefits register is a single living list of every benefit a program promised: what the benefit is, who owns it, how it will be measured, where it started, where it should end up, and where it stands today. An operations transition plan is the plan for handing the finished change to the people who will run it every day, so the benefit keeps arriving after the program team has gone. Together they answer two questions: are we still on track to get the benefit, and who will keep it alive once we leave? Think of a building project: the register is the running checklist of what the new building must deliver, and the transition plan is the handover to the facilities staff who will keep it working.
lessons.guessPrompt: A program finishes a new claims system on time and under budget, and the project team disbands. Six months later claims processing is slow again. What do you think went wrong, and what single plan or record could have prevented it?
lessons.teach: A benefit is the measurable value a change is meant to produce, such as faster claims or lower cost per order. The benefits register is the program's running record of every benefit: its description, owner, measure, baseline (the starting value), target (the value it should reach), forecast (the expected date or value), actual (what has been measured so far), and status. It is updated whenever new measurements or decisions arrive, so it always shows whether each benefit is still on track. The operations transition plan describes how the finished capability moves into day-to-day running: who takes ownership, what documentation, training, support and service levels are needed, what readiness criteria must be met before handover, and which sustainment metrics the operations owner will keep watching. Worked example: claims processing averages 10 days (baseline) against a target of 3 days. At month six the measured average is 4.5 days. You update the register: actual 4.5, gap 1.5 days, forecast revised from month 8 to month 9, and status amber with a corrective action assigned to the process owner. The transition plan then names that process owner as the benefit owner after closure. Common mistake: treating the register as a document that closes with the program, so no one outside the project watches the measure. Consequence: without an operations owner, the average can drift back toward 10 days, and the drift is usually noticed only when the sponsor asks why the investment has stopped paying off.

questions.prompt: A regional call centre tracks first-contact resolution, meaning the share of calls solved on the first call. The baseline is 62 percent and the target is 80 percent. At month five the measured figure is 71 percent. The team has recorded the actual as 71 percent, calculated the gap as 9 points, moved the forecast from month 9 to month 12, set the status to amber, and assigned a corrective action to the team lead for coaching. The programme closes next month. Which step must the operations transition plan add so that the measure keeps being watched after closure?
choices: Ask the sponsor to close the benefit line in the register as delivered at 71 percent.
Remove the benefit from the register, since the programme no longer funds it.
Reset the baseline to 71 percent so that future gaps look smaller.
Name the team lead as the benefit owner after closure, and write the measure and a sustainment threshold into the handover.
questions.why: The transition plan must name an operations owner who keeps watching the measure after the project ends, and the other choices either stop monitoring or distort the baseline.

questions.prompt: A benefits register for a warehouse shows a baseline of 340 minutes per shipment, a target of 200 minutes, and a current actual of 260 minutes. What is the gap that should be recorded?
choices: 80 minutes
140 minutes
200 minutes
60 minutes
questions.why: The gap is the distance between the current actual and the target, which is 260 minus 200, giving 60 minutes.

questions.prompt: A programme closes and its benefits register is archived. Nobody outside the project is named to watch the measure, which was a refund-processing time. Which outcome is most likely over the following year?
choices: The register updates itself with new measurements, so the drift is caught within a week.
The processing time drifts back toward its old level, and the drift is usually noticed late, when finance asks why the expected savings have stopped.
The processing time holds at target automatically because the new system enforces it.
The sponsor immediately starts a new programme to replace the lost benefit.
questions.why: Without an operations owner the measure is unwatched, so drift accumulates until someone outside the project notices the lost value.

questions.prompt: An online returns process has a baseline of 9 days and a target of 4 days. At month three a new measurement shows an average of 6.5 days. A team member proposes replacing the baseline with 6.5 so the gap looks smaller. What is the correct update to the register?
choices: Replace the target with 6.5 so the status turns green.
Delete the earlier measurement so the register shows only the current figure.
Keep the baseline at 9, record 6.5 as the actual, and show the gap as 2.5 days.
Replace the baseline with 6.5 and record the gap as zero.
questions.why: The baseline is the fixed starting value and must not be overwritten; the new measurement goes into actual and the gap is recalculated against the target.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is new to programs what a benefits register is and what an operations transition plan must contain. Then name one limit or tradeoff of relying on the register alone to guarantee that benefits are sustained.
lessons.modelAnswer: A benefits register is the program's live record of each promised benefit. For each one it holds the owner, the measure, the baseline, the target, the latest forecast and actual result, and a status, and we update it whenever new data arrives. An operations transition plan is what gets the finished change into daily running: it names who takes ownership, the documentation, training and support needed, the readiness criteria that must be met before handover, and the sustainment metrics the operations owner will monitor. The register alone is not enough to guarantee sustainment. It records what is happening but cannot make anyone act, and it usually stops being maintained once the program team disbands. The transition plan is what ties the measure to a permanent owner, so the register has someone to report to after closure.
rubricPoints: Defines the benefits register as a living record with owner, measure, baseline, target, forecast, actual and status
Describes the operations transition plan as handover of ownership, documentation, training and readiness criteria
Explains that the sustainment metrics must be watched by an operations owner after closure
Names a limit: the register records performance but does not force action or survive project closure without an owner

suggested.rationale: The core skill here is explaining how the register and transition plan connect, which no listed mission or planned engine currently covers.

lessons.plain: A program is a group of related projects managed together to deliver a benefit an organization wants. The people who can affect it, or be affected by it, are its stakeholders. Two roles matter most. The sponsor is the senior person who authorizes the program, provides funding, and is accountable for whether the benefit arrives. The steering committee is a small group of senior decision-makers who set direction, approve major changes, and settle disputes the program manager cannot resolve alone. Identifying them means listing everyone with a stake. A stakeholder matrix then records each person's influence, position, and the position the program needs, turning a list of names into a plan for where attention should go.
lessons.guessPrompt: A program to replace a regional dispatch system is funded by the finance director, will be used daily by dispatchers, and is opposed by a regional manager who fears losing control of his team. Without any reading, which of these three would you place on the steering committee, and why? Answer in a sentence or two.
lessons.teach:
A stakeholder is anyone who can affect a program or be affected by its outcome. A program is a set of related projects managed together to deliver a benefit that an organization wants, so it usually touches many people with different interests. Two roles need to be named early. The sponsor is the senior person who authorizes the program, provides funding and resources, and is accountable for whether the intended benefit is delivered. The steering committee is a small group of senior stakeholders who set direction, approve major changes, and resolve conflicts that the program manager cannot settle alone.

Why identify them and map their positions? Decisions made without knowing who holds power or who opposes the program tend to be reversed later. A stakeholder matrix is a table with one row per stakeholder. For each row you record their influence, their interest, their current position (for example supportive, neutral, or resistant), and the position the program needs them to hold. The gap between current and desired position shows where engagement effort should go.

Worked example. A program replaces a regional dispatch system. Step one: the finance director approves the budget, so she has high influence and is supportive; she is a sponsor. Step two: the operations head chairs the group that approves schedule changes; he joins the steering committee, is currently neutral, and must become supportive. Step three: a regional manager who fears losing control has high influence and is resistant, and needs to be at least neutral before go-live, so his row flags a specific engagement action.

Common mistake: treating the sponsor as the only stakeholder that matters, or listing names without positions, so the matrix becomes a contact list. On a running system, ignoring a resistant manager means his team keeps old workarounds, the new system goes live with low use, and the expected benefit never appears.

questions.prompt: A city transit authority runs a program to replace paper ticket validators with contactless card readers across its bus depots. Step one: the chief financial officer releases the capital budget and is answerable for the promised fare-revenue benefit, so she is the sponsor; her influence is high and her position is supportive. Step two: the operations chief chairs the panel that approves changes to the depot trial schedule, so he sits on the steering committee; his position is neutral and the program needs him supportive. Step three is missing: the depot maintenance manager has high influence over when the trial can start and is currently resistant, but his matrix row records only his current position. Which entry completes his row?
choices: Desired position: neutral before the trial, with a named action on his maintenance concerns
Leave the desired position blank until the steering committee meets
Desired position: supportive, copied from the chief financial officer's row
Desired position: resistant, since his team controls the depots
questions.why: The matrix must record the position the program needs, so the gap from resistant to at least neutral before the trial shows where engagement effort goes.

questions.prompt: In a program, which description best fits a steering committee?
choices: The single person who pays for the program and answers for its benefit
The delivery team that builds each individual project in the program
A small group of senior stakeholders who set direction, approve major changes, and settle conflicts the program manager cannot settle alone
Every person who will use the system once it goes live
questions.why: A steering committee is a small senior group that sets direction and resolves conflicts beyond the program manager, while the sponsor is a single person who funds the program and answers for its benefit.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm's warehouse automation program has one stakeholder who must approve any change to the go-live date, but who controls no budget and is not accountable for the benefit. Which role best fits this person?
choices: Program manager
Sponsor
Steering committee member
A stakeholder with no matrix entry needed
questions.why: A steering committee member approves major changes such as a schedule change, whereas the sponsor is the one who provides funding and answers for the benefit.

questions.prompt: A program manager's stakeholder matrix lists fourteen people with their influence and interest scores, but no current or desired positions for anyone. What is the main consequence for the running program?
choices: The steering committee has to be dissolved and rebuilt from scratch
Resistant stakeholders get no targeted effort, since nothing shows where current and desired positions differ
The influence scores stop being valid and must be discarded
The matrix becomes too short to meet governance expectations
questions.why: Without current and desired positions, the gap that shows where engagement should go cannot be seen, so a resistant stakeholder with high influence can be left unaddressed.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would identify the sponsor and steering committee for a new program and build a stakeholder matrix from that work. Name one limit or tradeoff of the matrix that they should keep in mind.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by listing everyone who can affect the program or be affected by it, then look at who authorizes and funds it. That person is the sponsor, and they are accountable for the benefit. For the steering committee, I would pick the few senior people who approve major changes and can settle disputes. Then I would build the matrix: one row per stakeholder, with influence, interest, current position, and the position we need them to reach. The gap between those two positions tells us where to focus. The main limit is that positions change, and the matrix is only a snapshot. It goes stale quickly, so it needs regular review, and I should not treat someone's listed position as fixed. It also reflects my judgment, so I should check it with the stakeholders themselves.
rubricPoints: Defines a sponsor as the accountable funder or authorizer of the program
Describes the steering committee as senior decision-makers for direction and disputes
Explains the matrix rows: influence, interest, current position, and desired position
Notes that the gap between current and desired positions drives engagement priorities
Names a limit such as the matrix going stale or reflecting judgment that needs validation

suggested.rationale: Applying the matrix to a messy stakeholder situation and justifying the placements adds the most beyond reading the definitions.

lessons.plain: Stakeholder analysis means working out who has a stake in a program, what each person cares about, how much power they have to help or block it, and what they already know or think about the work. Before you can plan how to keep people informed and involved, you need that picture. This objective is about gathering it from three kinds of sources: records of what happened on earlier projects, direct conversations with people, and the written agreements that give some people formal say. The output is a stakeholder engagement plan, which states for each group what you will do, who owns that action, and how you will know it is working.
lessons.guessPrompt: A program sponsor hands you a list of eight stakeholders and says the list is complete. Before you accept it, what two different kinds of evidence would you check, and why might the sponsor's list miss someone?
lessons.teach:
A stakeholder is any person or group who can affect the program or be affected by it. Stakeholder analysis is the structured work of identifying them and judging their interest, their influence, and their current attitude toward the program. Historical data means records from earlier programs, such as lessons-learned logs, issue histories, and notes on who actually drove or stalled past decisions. Interviews are structured one-to-one conversations used to hear concerns in the stakeholder's own words. Formal agreements are documents that fix someone's rights, such as a charter, a memorandum of understanding, or a contract clause that gives a group approval power. A stakeholder engagement plan turns the analysis into action: for each stakeholder it records the desired level of engagement, the gap from their current level, the action that closes the gap, an owner, and a review date.

Why this works: each source corrects the blind spots of the others. History shows who caused delays before, interviews reveal what people think now, and agreements show who holds decision rights on paper. When the three disagree, the disagreement is itself a finding worth acting on.

Worked example: a regional transit scheduling program. Past logs show that night-shift depot supervisors repeatedly stalled rollouts, yet they are not on the sponsor's list. Interviews reveal they fear losing overtime. A signed memorandum gives the union review rights over shift changes. Steps: add the supervisors and the union to the register; rate the supervisors as high interest and high practical influence; record their current engagement as resistant and their desired engagement as supportive; plan a pilot co-designed with them, owned by the operations manager, and reviewed monthly.

Common mistake: building the list once from the sponsor's memory and never revisiting it. Consequence: when the scheduling tool reaches the depots, the supervisors who were never analyzed keep the old paper rosters running, the new data feed goes unused, and the benefit case fails at cutover.

Engagement plans are living documents, so the analysis must be refreshed at each phase gate.

questions.prompt: A hospital network is moving patient scheduling to a new system. Past logs show that the night-shift charge nurses stalled two earlier go-lives, but they are missing from the current register. Interviews reveal they fear losing weekend staffing hours. A signed memorandum gives the nursing council consultation rights over shift patterns. The steps so far are: (1) add the charge nurses and the nursing council to the register; (2) rate the charge nurses as high interest and high practical influence; (3) step left out; (4) assign an owner and set a monthly review date. Which choice correctly completes step 3?
choices: Record their current engagement as opposed and their desired engagement as co-owning the change, then name the action that closes that gap
Copy the sponsor's ratings for all stakeholders so the plan stays consistent
Send one all-staff announcement so every nurse hears the same message at once
Remove the charge nurses from the register because the logs come from earlier programs
questions.why: Step 3 in an engagement plan records the gap between current and desired engagement and the action that closes it, which is what the choice describes.

questions.prompt: Which source in stakeholder analysis is the best place to find who holds decision rights on paper?
choices: Formal agreements, such as a charter or a contract clause, that fix approval power
Historical issue logs, because they record who has always made the final call on earlier programs
Interview notes from the first month, because people state their own authority in their own words and that is the most candid record available to a planner
The sponsor's personal recollection of who the key people are
questions.why: Formal agreements fix rights on paper, while interviews show current concerns and history shows who drove past decisions.

questions.prompt: A program builds its stakeholder list once from the sponsor's memory and never revisits it. Which outcome matches the consequence described in the teaching text?
choices: The register grows too long for the sponsor to read in full, which slows approval of the next phase
Groups that were never analyzed keep their old routines running, so the new data feed goes unused and the benefit case fails at cutover
Stakeholders volunteer their concerns earlier than the plan expected, so review meetings become unnecessary
Nothing changes in practice, because a sponsor's memory of the program tends to be accurate across every phase and every group involved
questions.why: The teaching text says unanalyzed groups keep old practices running, the new data goes unused, and the benefit case fails at cutover.

questions.prompt: A retail bank's branch managers delayed two earlier rollouts according to the logs. Current interviews show them supportive, and no formal agreement gives them approval rights. What should the planner do?
choices: Treat the disagreement as a finding and test current support against past delays before planning engagement
Write the managers into the charter with approval rights so the question closes
Ignore the history because only formal agreements count as evidence of influence
Trust the recent interviews and drop the older history as out of date
questions.why: The teaching text says that when the sources disagree, the disagreement is itself a finding worth acting on, so the planner should investigate it rather than pick one source.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would run a stakeholder analysis for a new program. Name the three sources you would draw on, and describe one limit or tradeoff of relying on interviews alone.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with the three sources together. Past program records show who actually held up earlier work, which the current sponsor may not remember. Interviews tell me what people care about now, and I would ask each person what would make them support or resist the program. Formal agreements tell me who has decision rights on paper, such as approval clauses or governance seats. I then combine them into a register with interest, influence, and current versus desired engagement for each person, and turn each gap into a named action with an owner. The main limit of interviews alone is that people describe their position with the most favorable framing, and they can miss influence that works informally. Someone who is not senior may still control a critical process. Checking interview claims against records and agreements is how I reduce that bias. The tradeoff is time: a thorough analysis takes longer, so I focus deeper effort on the high-influence stakeholders and keep the rest lighter, reviewing the whole register at each phase gate.
rubricPoints: Uses at least two of the three sources, historical data, interviews, and formal agreements, and says what each one contributes
Turns the analysis into an engagement plan with a current versus desired level, an action, and an owner for each stakeholder
Names a real limit of interviews, such as self-reported or biased views, and a way to check them
Notes that the analysis must be refreshed over time rather than done once

suggested.rationale: The core skill is reasoning about which sources to combine and explaining the tradeoffs, which is best checked by articulating it back rather than by a console task.

lessons.plain: When a program is meant to deliver a benefit, such as faster customer onboarding or lower costs, the people who care about it need to agree to back it and to know exactly how success will be measured. Negotiating support means working out what each stakeholder will give and get, often by trading scope, timing or resources. Setting expectations and acceptance criteria means writing down the measures (key performance indicators, or KPIs) and the conditions under which a benefit counts as delivered. It is like agreeing the scoreboard before the game starts, so nobody argues about the final score later.
lessons.guessPrompt: A sponsor says the program will be a success because customers will be happier. What is the first thing you would ask for before agreeing that this is a measurable benefit, and why?
lessons.teach:
A benefit is a measurable improvement the organisation gets because of a program, such as a shorter wait time or a lower cost per order. A key performance indicator (KPI) is a metric that tracks progress toward a benefit. A baseline is the starting value of that metric, measured before the program changes anything. Acceptance criteria are the agreed conditions that must be true before a benefit is accepted as delivered, including the measure, the target, the measurement method, the time window and who signs off. Stakeholder support is the willingness of people with influence, such as sponsors, funders and operational managers, to back the program with decisions and resources. Negotiation is the process of reaching an agreement in which each party gives something to get something.

It works because support lasts longer when each stakeholder can see what they will receive and how the result will be judged. A target everyone has agreed to, with a baseline and a named owner, removes the later argument about whether success happened.

Worked example. A program aims to cut customer onboarding time. Step 1: measure the baseline, which is the current median of 12 days from signup to first use, taken from six months of system data. Step 2: the finance director wants 5 days, while the operations head says 9 days is realistic given a vendor dependency. Step 3: the program manager negotiates a staged target of 9 days at the end of year one and 7 days at the end of year two, and the finance director agrees to fund phase two only if the phase one target is met. Step 4: the acceptance criteria are written down: median days from signup to first use, measured from the platform event log, averaged over three consecutive months, and signed off by the benefits owner.

Common mistake: agreeing a KPI in a meeting without a baseline or a measurement method, so the target sounds agreed but cannot be tested. In a running system this means the dashboard shows a number nobody can reconcile with the business view, and the sponsor withdraws support at the first disappointing report.

Written expectations and agreed acceptance criteria turn stakeholder support from a feeling into a shared, testable commitment.

questions.prompt: A regional hospital pharmacy wants to cut prescription pickup waits. Step 1 is done: the baseline is a median of 47 minutes from ticket creation to pickup, taken from three months of queue logs. Step 2 is done: the pharmacy director asks for 20 minutes, and the nursing lead says 35 minutes is realistic with current staffing. Step 3 is done: the program manager agrees a staged target of 35 minutes by month six, with funding for a refill-reminder module released only if that target is met. Step 4 is missing: the stakeholders have agreed the target but not yet written down how it will be tested. Which addition completes the acceptance criteria?
choices: Specify the measure, the measurement source and method (median minutes from ticket creation to pickup in the pharmacy queue system), the time window such as three consecutive months, and the named sign-off owner
Record the 47-minute baseline as the delivered benefit on the dashboard from day one so it is visible to everyone
Ask the pharmacy director to accept 20 minutes, since the baseline is already known and the gap is small
Average the waits from the final week of the program only, since that reflects how the pharmacy works now
questions.why: Acceptance criteria must state the measure, the measurement method, the time window and who signs off, which is what makes the agreed target testable later.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is a baseline in a benefits program run by a municipal water utility that wants to reduce unaccounted-for water loss?
choices: The total budget allocated to leak-detection crews over the program's life
The starting value of the loss metric, measured before the program changes anything
The average loss reported by neighbouring utilities in the same region
The target the utility commits to after the program ends, which is set by the board
questions.why: A baseline is the pre-program starting value of the metric, against which later progress is judged.

questions.prompt: An insurance firm's program sponsor agreed in a meeting to cut claim processing time by 30 percent. No one measured the current processing time, and no measurement method or sign-off owner was named. Six months later, the claims director says the program failed while the program team says it succeeded. What is the root problem?
choices: The 30 percent target was too ambitious for any insurance process
The team should have reported progress weekly instead of monthly
The agreed target could not be tested because it had no baseline, measurement method or owner
The sponsor should have funded more claims staff at the start of the program
questions.why: Without a baseline, a measure, a method and an owner, the target cannot be tested, so each side can claim a different result.

questions.prompt: A logistics company's operations head says the program sponsor's goal of same-day delivery in every district is not achievable within the current fleet. The sponsor insists on the original goal. Which negotiated outcome best fits the approach described for stakeholder support and expectations?
choices: Keep the original goal and tell the operations head to find the extra vehicles
Agree a staged target with a baseline, a measurement method and a named owner, linked to a funding decision at each stage
Drop the benefit entirely so the sponsor and operations head avoid further conflict
Let the operations head set the target alone and remove the sponsor from the decision
questions.why: Negotiation means each party gives something to get something, and staged, testable targets with clear measures let both sides see what they receive and how success is judged.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has just joined the program why we agree a KPI, its baseline and its acceptance criteria with stakeholders before the work starts, and name one limit or tradeoff of doing this.
lessons.modelAnswer: Before work starts, we agree the benefit, the KPI that tracks it, the baseline it is measured from, the target, the measurement method, the time window and the person who signs off. That gives sponsors and operational leaders a shared definition of success, so they support the program on the same terms and cannot reinterpret the result later. The tradeoff is that agreeing targets early takes negotiation time and often forces compromises, such as a staged target instead of the ambitious one a sponsor wanted. A KPI can also be met while the underlying benefit is not, so we need to review periodically whether the measure still reflects what the business actually cares about.
rubricPoints: Defines the benefit and the KPI that tracks it, with a baseline and a target.
States the acceptance criteria: measurement method, time window and sign-off owner.
Explains that agreed criteria turn stakeholder support into shared, testable expectations.
Names a tradeoff, such as negotiation time, compromised targets, or a metric that can be met without the benefit.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is explaining why agreed measures and negotiated support matter, which is best practised by explaining it back, and no listed mission or planned engine covers stakeholder negotiation.

lessons.plain: When people who will be affected by a program notice something that could go wrong, they often say so before the program team does. Those warnings are stakeholder-identified risks. A risk is an uncertain event that, if it happens, would help or hurt the program. The job is to take each warning, decide whether it is really a risk, judge how serious it is, decide what to do about it, and record it in the program's shared list of risks so it is watched like everything else. Ignoring a concern from a quiet or less powerful stakeholder is one of the most common ways programs get surprised late.
lessons.guessPrompt: A regional operations director tells you in a meeting that she is worried the new scheduling system will not work for night shifts. Nobody else has raised it. Before reading anything else, what would you do with that worry, and where would you record it?
lessons.teach:
A stakeholder-identified risk is a possible future event raised by someone outside the program team, such as a sponsor, a business unit leader, a regulator or an end user. Before it can be managed, it must be evaluated. Evaluation asks four questions. Is it really a risk, meaning an uncertain future event, rather than a problem that has already happened (an issue) or an assumption nobody has checked? How likely is it? How much would it affect the program's objectives and expected benefits? How soon could it occur? The answers set its priority against the other risks.

Once evaluated, the risk goes into the program risk register, the living list of risks, with a named owner and a planned response. Common responses are avoid (change the plan so it cannot happen), mitigate (reduce its likelihood or impact), transfer (shift it to another party, such as a vendor, through contract terms), accept (acknowledge it and set a trigger for action) or escalate (pass it up when it is beyond the program's authority). The program risk management plan sets how risks are handled across all component projects and benefits, so the stakeholder's risk must also be reflected there: who reviews it, how often, and which threshold sends it to the governance board.

Worked example: the director warns that the scheduling system may not handle night-shift rotations. Step 1: the team confirms it is a future event, not a fault already seen in testing, so it is a risk. Step 2: likelihood is medium, because the vendor's standard setup assumes day shifts. Step 3: impact is high, because night shifts cover a large share of staffed hours and the overtime benefit depends on them. Step 4: the integration lead owns it, the response is mitigate by adding a night-shift test scenario before the pilot, and a trigger is set so any failed night-shift test escalates to the governance board.

Common mistake: recording the concern only as a line in meeting minutes, or dismissing it because the person is not the sponsor. A risk nobody owns is not managed.

Consequence: if the risk is left out, the first sign is a failed rollout to night staff, a benefit slips, and the governance board hears about it late, when options are fewer and costs are higher. Stakeholder concerns belong in the risk register from the day they are raised.

questions.prompt: A regional finance controller warns that the new invoicing module may double-count supplier credits when a supplier is paid in two currencies. Step 1: the team confirms this is a possible future event, not a fault already seen in testing, so it is a risk. Step 2: likelihood is low to medium, because only a small share of suppliers are paid in two currencies. Step 3: impact is high, because a double-counted credit would misstate the quarterly close. Step 4 is missing. Which choice correctly completes step 4?
choices: Transfer it to the software vendor through the contract and remove it from the register.
Record the concern in the meeting minutes and revisit it after the pilot has produced more data.
Assign a named owner, choose a planned response, and reflect the risk in the program risk management plan with its review frequency and governance threshold.
Ask the sponsor to decide whether it counts as a risk, since the controller is not the sponsor.
questions.why: Step 4 must give the risk a named owner and a planned response and make sure the program risk management plan sets how the risk is reviewed and when it goes to the governance board.

questions.prompt: A logistics manager tells the program team that a warehouse scanner server crashed last Tuesday and some dispatch records were lost. How should the team classify this item before evaluating it?
choices: As a risk, because it might happen again next month.
As a benefit, because it will help the team find weak points.
As an assumption, because nobody has checked the cause yet.
As an issue, because the event has already happened.
questions.why: An issue is a problem that has already occurred, whereas a risk is an uncertain future event, so a crash that already happened is an issue rather than a risk.

questions.prompt: A regulator warns that a new reporting feature could miss a filing deadline if the build slips. The program team decides to move the reporting feature into a later release window, so the slip cannot affect the filing date. Which planned response does this describe?
choices: Transfer, because the risk was shifted to another party.
Accept, because the team acknowledged the risk and set a trigger.
Avoid, because the plan was changed so the risk cannot occur.
Mitigate, because the team reduced the likelihood of the slip.
questions.why: Avoid means changing the plan so the risk cannot happen, and moving the feature out of the deadline window does exactly that, whereas mitigation would only lower its likelihood or impact.

questions.prompt: A business unit leader's concern about a training rollout risk has been entered in the program risk register with an owner and a response. However, the program risk management plan says nothing about how often this risk is reviewed or what threshold sends it to the governance board. What is the gap?
choices: The response should be changed to transfer, since the business unit leader raised it.
The program risk management plan does not yet reflect the stakeholder risk, so review frequency and escalation threshold are missing.
The risk was never a real risk, so it should be removed from the register.
The owner should be replaced by the sponsor, because only sponsors can own risks.
questions.why: The program risk management plan must reflect each stakeholder-identified risk, including who reviews it, how often, and which threshold sends it to governance, so the missing review rules are the gap.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would take a risk raised by a stakeholder and bring it into the program risk management plan. Name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would first confirm the concern is a genuine future risk rather than an issue or an untested assumption, then score its likelihood and impact against the program's objectives and benefits so it can be compared with the other risks. I would give it a named owner, pick a response such as mitigate, transfer, accept or escalate, and record it in the program risk register. Then I would check that the program risk management plan covers it, meaning its review cadence and the escalation threshold that sends it to governance. The tradeoff is effort: evaluating every stakeholder concern thoroughly takes time the team may not have, so I would triage by impact and urgency and log minor concerns with a lighter review. The limit is that my scoring depends on the stakeholder's information, so I would validate it with data before committing budget to a response.
rubricPoints: Confirms the concern is a future, uncertain event rather than an issue or an unchecked assumption.
Scores likelihood and impact against program objectives and expected benefits.
Assigns a named owner and a response such as avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept or escalate.
Records the risk in the program risk register and reflects it in the program risk management plan, including review cadence and escalation triggers.
Names a tradeoff, such as evaluation effort versus coverage, or reliance on the stakeholder's own information.

suggested.rationale: Judging whether a stakeholder concern is a real risk and what to do with it is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style scenario, which adds more than any listed mission.

lessons.plain: Stakeholders are the people and groups who are affected by a program or who can influence whether it succeeds. Developing and fostering relationships with them means building trust over time, so they understand what the program is doing, feel heard, and keep backing it when things get difficult. It is not a single meeting or a status email. It is a steady pattern of two-way conversation, where you listen as much as you inform and adjust your approach to each person's concerns. Think of a plant manager who reads every update but never agrees to anything until she feels her team's worries have been taken seriously.
lessons.guessPrompt: A program sponsor approves a major change, then stops returning calls and quietly stops defending the program in leadership meetings. What do you think went wrong in the relationship, and what could have been done earlier to prevent it?
lessons.teach:
A stakeholder is anyone who can affect the program or be affected by it, such as sponsors, senior executives, business unit leaders, and the people who will use the new capability. Stakeholder engagement is the set of actions you take to understand these people and involve them. Fostering a relationship means keeping that engagement going across the whole life of the program, so that support is sustained rather than borrowed at the start.

Why it works: people support what they understand and what they feel they had a say in. Trust is built through repeated, honest, two-way contact. When you listen to a concern and then act on it, or explain clearly why you cannot, the other person learns that their input counts. That credibility is what carries a program through funding reviews, scope disputes and delays.

Worked example. A program is consolidating three regional reporting systems. The operations director for the north region is skeptical. Step 1: you learn from her peers that she believes the change will remove her team's control over their own data. Step 2: you meet her one-to-one, not in the program's senior governance group, and ask what she needs to see. Step 3: you acknowledge the concern and show how the design keeps her team as owners of their data. Step 4: you agree a fortnightly check-in and record what she asked for and what you delivered. Over three months her tone shifts from objection to proposing improvements.

Common mistake: treating engagement as broadcasting. Sending more status reports is not the same as being heard, and a stakeholder who feels ignored will stop reading them.

Consequence: when relationships are thin, one setback, such as a slipped benefit date, can turn a quiet skeptic into an active blocker, and the program loses the support it needs to recover. Sustained, two-way engagement is what keeps a program funded and moving.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm is moving warehouse stock tracking onto one shared platform. The program manager has already done three things with the Leeds depot manager, who fears the central team will take over her stock adjustments. Step 1: she asked the depot manager's supervisor what the worry was. Step 2: she met the depot manager one-to-one and asked what she needed to see. Step 3: she added the adjustment-approval control the depot manager asked for and told her when it was live. The depot manager now asks for a second change, a bulk-import feature, which cannot be built in this release. Which step completes the response to this second request?
choices: Explain clearly why the bulk-import feature cannot be built this release, agree when it will be revisited, and record that agreement.
Escalate the request to the steering group so the feature is forced into this release.
Send the depot manager the full weekly status pack with the bulk-import request marked as noted.
Tell the depot manager the request is refused and close the item in the change log.
questions.why: Acting on a concern or explaining clearly why it cannot be acted on, then recording the agreement, is what shows the stakeholder that their input counts, which the other options fail to do.

questions.prompt: Which of these best fits the course's definition of a stakeholder?
choices: A regulator outside the company whose approval can stop the go-live.
Only the people who fund the program and sign off its budget.
Only the people who approve the monthly program report.
Only the project staff who write and test the code.
questions.why: A stakeholder is anyone who can affect the program or be affected by it, and an outside regulator can stop the go-live, so it qualifies while the other narrower groups do not.

questions.prompt: A program manager emails a 20-page status pack every Friday to a regional supervisor, who never replies. Three months later the supervisor publicly opposes the rollout. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The supervisor is hostile by nature and cannot be engaged at all.
The program should have escalated to the sponsor sooner.
The status pack was too short to show the program's progress.
Sending reports was treated as engagement, so the supervisor never felt heard.
questions.why: Broadcasting status reports without two-way contact is a common mistake, and a stakeholder who feels ignored will stop reading them and may turn into an opponent.

questions.prompt: Two stakeholders are each told about the same six-week benefit slip. Stakeholder X has had regular one-to-one contact, and earlier concerns were acted on or explained. Stakeholder Y has only received written updates. Which is most likely to stay supportive, and why?
choices: Both equally, because the same slip affects each of them in the same way.
X, because a senior person is naturally more forgiving of delays than others.
Y, because written updates keep stakeholders informed without placing pressure on them.
X, because past two-way contact built credibility that carries the program through setbacks.
questions.why: Trust built through repeated, honest, two-way contact is what carries a program through setbacks such as delays, so the stakeholder with that history is the more likely to remain supportive.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why keeping a sponsor's support over the life of a program takes more than regular status reports. Name one limit or tradeoff of relationship-building that they should watch for.
lessons.modelAnswer: Status reports push information one way, so they tell a sponsor what happened but not what they think or fear. Sustained support comes from two-way contact: I learn what each stakeholder cares about, act on what they raise, and tell them plainly when I cannot, so they trust that their input has an effect. The tradeoff is time. One-to-one conversations take hours that could go to delivery, and with many stakeholders I cannot give everyone the same depth. So I prioritise the people with the most influence over benefits and funding, record what each asked for and what we did, and rely on regular forums for everyone else. A watch-out is that trust built on one person can vanish when that person leaves, so I spread the relationship across more than one contact.
rubricPoints: Status reports are one-way, while sustained support depends on two-way, trust-building contact.
Stakeholders need to see that their concerns are heard and acted on, or explained when not possible.
A real tradeoff exists: relationship time competes with delivery time across many stakeholders.
Relationships concentrated in one person are fragile, so trust should be spread across several contacts.

suggested.rationale: Explaining the difference between informing and sustaining support, and naming a tradeoff, is the core skill here and no listed mission or engine covers stakeholder relationships.

lessons.plain: A program is a group of related projects that together aim at a bigger business result than any one project could deliver alone. Developing program management standards and structure means deciding, before the work gets busy, how that program will be run: who makes which decisions, which rules and templates everyone follows, how money is tracked, which shared tools are used, and how progress is reported upward. Think of it as setting up the scaffolding and house rules for a large building project so that many crews can work without constantly asking who is in charge or how invoices should look. Good structure is set up early and kept light enough that teams still move quickly.
lessons.guessPrompt: Three project teams inside one program each send their own status report, in a different format and on a different day, so the sponsor cannot compare them. What single thing should the program have set up earlier, and who should own it?
lessons.teach:
A program management office (PMO) is the group that maintains the program's standards, tools, and reporting so that individual project managers do not each invent their own. Governance means the rules about who decides what, and at what level. A governance board is the group with authority to approve program-level changes, such as moving money between projects or accepting a big scope change. Standards are the agreed templates, definitions, and methods every project follows. Finance here means how the program's budget is planned, approved, and tracked across all its components. Reporting is the regular, consistent information that flows from projects to the program and from the program to the board. Tools are the shared systems for schedules, risk logs, and documents.

This works because consistency lets leaders compare components side by side, and clear decision rights stop small questions from stalling in a queue. Consider a program with three projects: a billing upgrade, a new customer portal, and a data migration. Step 1: the program manager defines one status template with five fields: scope, schedule, cost to date against budget, top risks, and decisions needed. Step 2: finance requires each project to book spend to a shared cost code, so program totals add up. Step 3: the board fixes a monthly reporting date and states that any change above an agreed threshold comes to it for approval. Step 4: the PMO keeps one risk log that all three projects use. In month two, the board sees three reports that line up, and a cost overrun in the portal appears in the same place as the billing project's, so the pattern is visible early.

The common mistake is writing a heavy standards set on day one, copied from another organization, that teams ignore, or leaving reporting formats to each project so that leaders cannot compare them. When projects use their own cost codes, the program total is wrong at the next board meeting, and funding decisions get made on numbers that do not reconcile.

questions.prompt: A regional water utility runs three pipe-replacement projects. Step 1: the program office issues one status template with five fields: scope, schedule, spend against budget, top risks, and decisions needed. Step 2: finance requires each project to book its spend to a shared cost code. Step 3: the governance board sets a threshold of 250,000 for any budget change, and anything above it comes to the board for approval. Step 4 is the one left out of the setup notes. In each monthly cycle, what should the program office do with the three reports before the board meets?
choices: Hold all reports until every project manager has written a full narrative.
Replace the fixed monthly date with a call whenever a project feels it has news.
Forward each project's report unchanged so the board sees the original figures.
Reconcile each project's spend to the shared cost codes and flag mismatches before totals go to the board.
questions.why: Checking the spend against the shared cost codes before totals are presented keeps the program figures reconciled, which is the purpose of the shared code in the first place.

questions.prompt: In a program, what is the main job of the governance board?
choices: Writing the detailed daily task lists for each project team
Auditing the program office's own staff hours each quarter
Approving program-level changes such as moving money between projects
Setting up the shared document system and the risk log
questions.why: The governance board is the group with authority to approve program-level changes, while day-to-day tasks and tools belong to projects and the program office.

questions.prompt: A program has two projects. One project's finance staff book their costs to a local code instead of the shared cost code. What is the most likely consequence at the next board meeting?
choices: The board automatically approves a higher budget for that project
The program office replaces the standards with a longer template
That project's schedule slips by the amount of the unbooked cost
The program total does not reconcile, so funding decisions rest on wrong numbers
questions.why: Costs booked outside the shared code are missing from the program totals, so the totals the board uses for funding decisions do not reconcile.

questions.prompt: A new program office adopts a 60-page standards set copied from a much larger organization on its first day. Which outcome is most likely?
choices: Every project immediately adopts the standards and reporting becomes faster
The board rejects the program budget because the standards are too long
Teams ignore most of the set and each project reports in its own way
The standards work well because more detail always gives better comparisons
questions.why: A heavy standards set imported on day one tends to be ignored, and when projects report in their own ways, leaders cannot compare them side by side.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would set up the governance structure, reporting, and finance standards for a new program in its first month. Name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you choose, such as how much standardization to impose on projects with different needs.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by writing down who holds decision rights: a governance board for program-level changes, the program manager for day-to-day calls across projects, and project managers for their own schedules. Then I would adopt one reporting template and one reporting date for all projects, with a short list of measures the board reads every time. For finance, I would require every project to use shared cost codes and a single budget baseline, so the totals reconcile. Tools come last: I would pick one risk log and one schedule view and avoid adding more. The tradeoff is that heavy standards slow small, low-risk projects down, so I would set a threshold below which lighter reporting applies, and I would review the standards after the first two reporting cycles.
rubricPoints: Names the governance board or decision rights and what level decides what
Describes one common reporting template and cadence so projects can be compared
Explains shared cost codes or a single baseline so financial totals reconcile
Names a tradeoff, such as too much standardization slowing small projects

suggested.rationale: The core skill is explaining how program standards, decision rights, and finance fit together and what they cost, and no listed mission or planned engine covers this.

lessons.plain: A governance framework is the agreed set of rules for how a program is steered: who makes which decisions, which meetings and checkpoints take place, and where problems go when they are too big for the team to solve. Selecting one means choosing or adapting that set so it fits the rules the wider organization already requires, such as spending limits, audit trails, and reporting deadlines. Think of it like choosing house rules for a shared building: they must respect the building's fire code, even if your household prefers different habits. A good program manager can explain why each rule exists and show where it comes from.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your program will spend money in three phases. The parent organization says any spending above a set amount needs finance sign-off before the next phase starts. Would you choose a governance setup that lets the program team approve its own spending, or one that builds in a finance sign-off? Why?
lessons.teach:
A governance framework is the documented structure a program uses to make and control decisions: the decision bodies, the decision rights (the explicit list of which decisions each role may make alone and which need someone else), the review points, and the escalation paths for problems. A governance board is the group with authority to approve, change or stop the program. Organizational governance requirements are the rules the parent organization already imposes, such as approval thresholds, audit obligations and reporting cadence. Conforming means the framework you select satisfies every one of those requirements, not only the ones you find convenient.

Why it works: the organization cannot watch every program closely, so it relies on written rules that are checked at predictable points. A framework that matches those rules lets the organization trust the program's decisions without re-checking each one.

Worked example. Step 1: list the requirements from the parent policy: spending above 500,000 needs finance and executive sign-off; a quarterly report goes to the portfolio committee; severe risks must be escalated within five working days. Step 2: map each requirement to a framework element: a finance seat on the governance board, a stage-gate review before each phase, and an escalation policy with a severity threshold and a time limit. Step 3: check for gaps. The draft lets team leads release 300,000 purchases each without review, so add a rule that aggregated commitments count toward the threshold. Step 4: record the mapping so an auditor can trace each rule back to its source.

Common mistake: choosing a framework because a previous program used it or because it looks thorough, then discovering it skips a required approval. Consequence: money gets committed without the required sign-off, which can produce an audit finding and force the program to unwind decisions at its next gate.

A framework is only as sound as its traceable match to the organization's rules, and a framework that cannot show that match has not yet been properly selected.

questions.prompt: A city transit authority is electrifying its bus depots. The parent policy sets three rules: any single contract above 250,000 needs sign-off from the chief financial officer and the transit board; a monthly report goes to the board's audit committee; any safety-critical risk must be escalated within 3 working days. The program team maps these to framework elements. Step 1: list the requirements above. Step 2: map them: a finance seat on the governance board, a stage-gate review before each phase, and an escalation policy with a safety-critical severity level and a 3-day limit. Step 3 is missing: the draft lets each of four depot leads sign purchase orders of 90,000 directly, with no review. Step 4: record the mapping so an auditor can trace each rule to its source. What rule must be added at Step 3 to close the gap?
choices: Count purchases from the same program together toward the 250,000 threshold, so the combined 360,000 needs CFO and board sign-off.
Add a monthly audit report to the transit board, since the audit committee has not yet been covered.
Nothing is needed, because each order is under 250,000 and so the draft already conforms.
Raise each depot lead's individual limit to 100,000 so that every order looks visibly small.
questions.why: The requirement applies to the program's total commitment, so separate small orders that add up above the threshold must be aggregated and reviewed, which is the gap the draft leaves open.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, which element is the group with authority to approve, change or stop a program?
choices: A stakeholder register that lists who is affected by the program
A change request form that records proposed scope changes
A governance board
A risk log that lists every open threat and its owner
questions.why: A governance board is defined in the teaching text as the group with authority to approve, change or stop the program, while the other three are documents or records, not decision-making bodies.

questions.prompt: A small research program is starting under a new parent policy that requires finance sign-off on any purchase over 100,000. The team's project lead wants to reuse the framework from their last program, which has no finance seat. What is the correct response?
choices: Map each parent policy requirement to a framework element, and add a finance sign-off step before any commitment above 100,000.
Drop the threshold rule, because this program is smaller than the last one.
Ask the finance team to look at purchases informally after they have been made.
Keep the previous framework, since it worked on the last program.
questions.why: Conforming means the selected framework satisfies every organizational requirement, which requires mapping each rule to an element and closing gaps before commitments are made, not relying on past success or after-the-fact review.

questions.prompt: A program's framework has a stage gate before each phase and a monthly steering meeting.
